BasePK: 3909579

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, the whole point of this referendum legislation, and especially the current process headed by Mr. Clark, is that the federal government will try and settle the constitutional question once and for all.
The hon. member knows perfectly well that all the energy being spent on the constitutional question would be better spent on economic issues and on finding jobs for Quebecers and Canadians.
I think the time has come to terminate the process. If we think a referendum should be held, we will do it, but it is not a binding referendum. However, we see it as a device that could bring the whole constitutional process to a conclusion.
This is only one phase. We have gone through several phases, as I mentioned in my speech. However, it is one phase we would prefer to avoid. If this week in Montreal or next week in Toronto, Mr. Clark's group were to reach an agreement, it would be a relief. Quebec would be able to hold its referendum, and everything would be fine.
However, if there is no agreement, I think it only makes sense for the government to consider all the options. I think it stands to reason that a democratic country like Canada should go to the people.

BasePK: 3909581

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, personally, I would prefer to see spending limits in this kind of bill. However, officials of the federal Department of Justice were unanimous in their opinion that if people were forced to associate under the aegis of two umbrella-committees-which would be the only way to limit spending, because one could then limit the spending of these committeess-and if this were challenged before the courts, the group or person initiating the challenge would have an excellent chance of winning their case. If this were to happen during a referendum period, we have no way of knowing what the courts would do. The court might decide that the clause in question was ultra vires or it might decide that the bill itself was ultra vires, which could have disastrous consequences.
To answer the questions raised by the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier and the hon. member for Saint-Denis, at the committee stage we intend to call as witnesses the people who gave us these legal opinions. At that stage, either my colleagues will be convinced, or if members of the two opposition parties have a better idea that would make it possible to get around this legal point, then, as the government House leader said, we are prepared to improve the bill in order to obtain the broadest possible consensus among members of this House.
May 19, 1992

The decision handed down last Friday is just as harmful and irrational as all the other decisions that were made since 1986. The industry is dying while the government watches the parade. Even with this reduction, the industry will lose $200 million this year.

Mr. Speaker, on the issue of funding for fee payers under section 26, this, by the way, is the amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act which she and the Liberal Party vehemently opposed. These are the same people complaining in this House today about a measure they fought for a year and a half. Let us get that straight.
On the issue of funding, last year there was $43 million under section 26 just for Ontario. We are increasing that amount to $125 million in 1992. That is almost three times as much as was spent in 1991. Because of the needs and demands on this program, yes we have to be more selective. We will be in order to ensure that in the end

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, the minister talks about being selective and the fact that it will be possible to be selective with these new constraints on training.
Does the minister think it is being selective when in Windsor it is not going to be possible for a single extra person to take training under section 26?
Is it being selective when the people at the Canada Employment Centre say they need $2 million more to cover the desperate needs of people in Windsor?
I ask this minister to get serious and to start doing something for the people of this country.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, the United States export enhancement program has cost Canadian grain producers $1.8 billion over the last five years. If there is no agreement reached in the Uruguay round of negotiations by June of this year, the United States plans to expand its export enhancement program by $1 billion to $2 billion in the next crop year.
I want to ask the Minister of Agriculture what action the government is going to take, whether the Prime Minister is going to be raising this matter and taking action with the President of the United States in his meetings tomorrow and with the European Community so that we do not have a violent escalation of the export enhancement program and the destruction of thousands of Canadian grain and oilseeds producers and fanners.

BasePK: 3909725

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, what I put forward today with all sincerity was a formula that I believe would work better than simply having a national majority. Some members in the House advocate that British Columbia ought to be a region in itself. Some advocate that the two territories should be another region. I suppose we can have those debates without any final resolution.
I am trying also to inject a dose of practicality into it. We may be in a national referendum this summer or early fall.
What we are attempting to do is try to avoid the Meech Lake process that not only failed many Canadians in the substance but failed miserably in the process. Canadians felt that they were disenfranchised by a constitution they thought they owned, given that is the premier law of this land. We are saying that there happens to be 27 million shareholders of this public company called Canada and we should no long rely simply on the chairman of the board or the chief executive officer or the board of directors to have a strong voice. We are suggesting it is time for all Canadians to have that voice. Putting in a prerequisite for a double majority as defined by those four regions would further solidify the feeling of unity and belonging to this country. It is certainly far superior than having 50 plus one pass the post.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member had been listening to my comments earlier, he would have heard me say that because of clear examples in the past of referendums that were very divisive, I generally did not support it. In fact, I could easily oppose the whole concept of referendums.
Having said that, since we have had a very clear indication in this country that people want input, through this bill, they will be given the opportunity to do that.
He may not like the tyranny of the majority. All I would say to him is that in this country, either you have tyranny of the minority or tyranny of the majority, or hopefully we have a deal that all Canadians will

cherish and we do not need to ask them the question in the first place.

BasePK: 3909752

Speech:
We can obviously not rely solely on the discretion of the Prime Minister. He has neither the credibility nor the support at this point in time to carry the constitutional issue through on his own.
Canada's interest transcends political parties. It is in that context that the Leader of the Opposition has been talking for over a year now about the need for co-operation between the three major national parties in order to resolve the constitutional crisis.
To my great regret, I must say that, unfortunately, opposition parties were not consulted at all on this bill. We have been called to the office of the government House leader only to be told: "Here is what it will be." There was no consultation, only a briefing.
Under the circumstances, we deeply deplore this move on the part of government. If this is any indication of what it has in store for the weeks to come, it tells you this is scary, very scary, because we feel that the interest of Canada should obviously take precedence over that of political parties. It seems to me that the Prime Minister of Canada is more concerned by his self-interest and his political survival than by the best interest of this country when he brings forward a bill such as this one.
I think that the points made about the Canadian Charter of Rights are totally preposterous and superfluous. I will refer to an article by Michel Auger published on May 16 in Le Journal de Montreal which state, regarding this argument: "Prime Minister Mul-roney said on Thursday that the government would have gladly used the Quebec model, with two umbrella committees, for its own referendum on the Constitution, but the Charter prevents it."
The Lortie commission looked into the matter. I must remind my hon. colleagues that this commission worked for two years and made very specific recommendations based on legal opinions paid for by the Conservative government which state clearly that it is possible to limit expenses incurred by a third party for an election or by umbrella committees for a referendum without contravening the charter.
May 19, 1992

I would suggest that the Prime Minister and the government House leader refer to the Lortie report to make sure that the legal opinions provided by the lawyer they have paid to assist the Lortie commission are not ignored. It seems obvious to me that the charter clearly says that the citizens have rights, but it also says in its first section that freedoms are not absolute and can be subject to such reasonable limits as can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society.
During the weekend, Professor Mendes of the University of Western Ontario law school, faxed me his legal opinion in which he explained in great detail how the charter can limit certain expenses in the case of a referendum legislation. He referred particularly to the recent decision of Justice Sopinka in the Queen v. Butler. I will read this paragraph of his legal opinion:

I would suggest that the appropriate standard is that laid down by Justice Sopinka in the R v. Butler decision that Parliament is entitled to have "a reasonable apprehension of harm" resulting from the dangers which the legislation is attempting to avoid.
"It would be quite easy for the government to have proved in an appeal from Justice Medhurst's decision"- and this is the decision that was rendered in Alberta at the time of the 1984 election-that the Conservative government did not want to appeal. It should have appealed. The chief electoral officer asked the government to appeal and it never wanted to appeal.
This decision is quite clear, that "there is a reasonable apprehension of harm resulting from unlimited spending during elections or referendums".
Professor Mendes concludes by saying:
Perhaps the reasons why the government did not appeal Justice Medhurst's decision and why they do not wish to put spending limits in any referendum legislation have nothing to do with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms or with law at all.

In a nutshell, Mr. Speaker, those are the comments that I wanted to make at this point. It seems obvious to me that this bill, while it is desirable in itself, will have to be seriously amended if it wants to get the attention and the credibility that it needs.
Private Members' Business
I note that the member for Edmonton-Southwest spoke earlier in this House. He reminded quite appropriately that the parliamentary committee he co-chaired with Senator Beaudoin specifically recommended to the government of Canada, should it want to get a consensus on constitutional amendments or should it fail to agree with the 10 provincial governments, to submit to the people a constitutional agreement which could be supported by at least a majority of the provinces representing more than 50 per cent of the Canadian population.
It seems to me that this last resort approach of consulting the population to tell us whether or not our constitutional proposal is valid and acceptable and in the best interests of Canada is something that must be done, but it must be done properly, with very strict rules of election spending limits and also with umbrella committees for the yes side and the no side.
Observers will recognize that referendum legislations is historically common.
One was submitted to the Parliament of London to determine whether or not England should join the Common Market. On the yes side was a major group composed of all sorts of people and of all political allegiances. The same can be said for the no side. BasePK: 3909805

Speech:
The medical profession in my home province of British Columbia is being blind-sided by two pieces of provincial legislation brought down by the NDP government. Bills C-13 and C-14 attempt to cap the earnings of and eliminate the pension contributions for physicians in B.C.
This unilateral action by the government threatens to limit the access of British Columbians to quality health care, alienates the medical profession, creates longer waiting lists and forces doctors out of B.C.
It is obviously unjust to require specialists such as a radiologist who purchases high tech, high-priced equipment for one's practice to come under the same earning limits as the low overhead physician.
The province has not consulted with the BCMA and refuses to negotiate a more equitable settlement even now. This unilateral action jeopardizes the historically co-operative relationship between the medical profession and the government.
I call on the federal government to take whatever action is necessary under the Canada Health Act to force the B.C. government to resume meaningful negotiations with the doctors of British Columbia.

BasePK: 3909813

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, a few minutes ago, the Prime Minister and the President of the United States held a news conference in Washington. The Prime Minister has travelled to the U.S. to deal first-hand wi th some of the trade irritants which have arisen out of the latest round of American protectionism.
Right now, a lot of Canadians are wondering about the future of free trade, given the disputes over softwood lumber, Honda cars, and so on. So it was reassuring to hear President Bush a few moments ago say that since the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement was signed in 1988, the trade between the two countries has grown by over $30 billion. That is thirty thousand million dollars of additional trade since free trade and that translates into more jobs on both sides of the border. Those are the facts.
The economic recession which has bedevilled both countries would likely have been a lot deeper if it had not been for those $30 billion.
Of course problems remain. The trade deal can be improved. Americans' attitudes can be improved. If there is one person who can do it, he is in Washington today.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak to this motion concerning the role of the Security Intelligence Review Committee, also known as the SIRC within the national security system.
In 1984, the Canadian Security Intelligence Service (CSIC) Act and the Security Offences Act established a new legislative framework to govern Canada's national security system.
The new legislation was designed to create a balanced and accountable system for the protection of Canada's national security interests and the preservation of the democratic way of life of its people. It provided the main legislative framework for the national security system, assigning security intelligence to CSIS, and confirmed

May 20, 1992

the security enforcement and the protective security mandate of the RCMP.
Embodied in the legislation was a set of interlocking principles to shape and guide the operation of the system and each principle can be associated with one of its major participants.
The legislation incorporated a clear mandate and strict controls of the activities of the new service. The inclusion of ministerial oversight and sophisticated review mechanisms ensured that the service would be effective and that the rights of individuals would be respected. Balance was a distinguishing feature of the legislation.
The need to protect national security was balanced by respect for individual rights and freedoms. The need to provide the service with sufficient powers to produce effective security intelligence was balanced by statutory controls and policy direction.
The need for CSIS to employ certain intrusive techniques was balanced by the requirement for prior authorization by a minister of the Crown and the Federal Court. The need for secrecy was balanced by ministerial accountability and informed independent review.
The national security system assigned specific and distinct mandates to CSIS and the RCMP. The service's primary mandate is to be found in two provisions of the CSIS act: the definition of "threats to the security of Canada", and the description of the service's duty to collect, analyse and retain information and intelligence on "threats to the security of Canada".
In order to fulfill its mandate the service undertakes counter-terrorism and counter-intelligence investigations of various types and duration.
The CSIS mandate is conditioned by the limits and controls specified in the act, by ministerial directions, and by the service's own operational policies and procedures. Certain powers employed by the service are subject to the requirement to obtain a judicial warrant.
In view of the complexity of CSIS activities and the importance of securing public confidence in the integrity of the system, the CSIS act provides for an independent external review body, the SIRC, reporting to Parliament through the Solicitor General on the activities of the service. The act also establishes the function of the inspector general to conduct independent internal reviews of the service for the Solicitor General
Like other government departments and agencies,
CSIS is required to pursue its objectives with full respect for the law including the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
Legislation governing the creation of a security intelligence agency has a special need for a policy framework, if there is to be public confidence in how the agency operates. Ministerial direction helps to ensure that the Solicitor General, who is accountable to Parliament, is the linchpin in the legal and policy framework.
The principles of ministerial control and accountability are central to Canadian parliamentary democracy. The CSIS Act ensured that the minister would have full knowledge and power of direction over the policies, operations and management of CSIS and also supplies the minister with the means to control and guide the service.
The function of the inspector general forms an integral part of the over-all accountability process. The CSIS Act established the inspector general's reporting role to the minister.
The terms of the act assign the inspector general a review and a monitoring function with respect to CSIS, and no information other than cabinet confidences may be withheld on any grounds.
By serving the minister directly, the inspector general maintains a measure of distance from the minister's policy and operational advisors in the ministry secretariat.
Canadian are protected by limitations in the CSIS mandate and the scope of prescribed activities of the service, by the conditions of the warrant process and the complaint and review processes provided in the act.
In the performance of its duties and functions, CSIS has no authority to counter or deter threats to the security of Canada. Investigations are to be initiated only when suspicions are based on "reasonable grounds", and the investigations themselves are to be conducted in a reasonable manner.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate on Bill C-81.
I support the principle of this bill and I emphasize the principle of the bill because I see flaws in it. I would like to discuss those flaws and my concerns in a moment.
It is clear Canadians want to be consulted on the matter of constitutional change. They want a say in the reshaping of our fundamental laws and we in the Liberal Party believe Canadians deserve nothing less. That is why we support a national referendum. After all the Constitution is not owned by politicians; it belongs to the people of Canada.
People are saying they do not want another Meech Lake. No more secret, late night meetings; Canadians must be full partners in the process.
I want to get to some of the reservations I have about this bill because I believe, as do my colleagues on this side of House, that the bill can be improved considerably. We sincerely hope that the government will consider amendments very seriously at the committee stage examination of this bill.
It is unfortunate that we are discussing this bill now. There has been an unfortunate delay concerning referendum legislation. After all our leader proposed a referendum one year ago. There have been all kinds of signals from across Canada, including signals from a couple of parliamentary committees, for the need of having a referendum tied to any constitutional change.
Unfortunately the government sat on its hands and did nothing. Now at this very late hour, when there is what you might call a bit of panic in the country, we have Bill C-81 before us. It is really unfortunate that the govem-

ment did not bring forward this legislation, if not months ago certainly weeks ago.
Let us take a look at some of the other concerns that we have on this side of the House. This legislation, Bill C-81, provides for a referendum but only on an optional basis. In other words it does not make a referendum mandatory before proceeding to any constitutional change. I believe that is unfortunate.
We know that the Constitution does not require referenda before changes are made. I am aware of that. We can certainly have legislation in this House that ties our hands, that binds parliamentarians to having a referendum and observing its results before we proceed toward constitutional change. It is very unfortunate that this legislation provides for a referendum but only as an option. There is also the question of the question. There is nothing in this bill that sets out the question. There is nothing in this bill that provides us as parliamentarians with a full role in the determination of what the question is. From my reading of this bill, the question will be left to the determination of the government. Again that is very unfortunate.
If we are going to have fairness in the process, if we are going to have Canadians supporting the process, then Canadians will want to see full participation of all parliamentarians, not just the government. It is unfortunate that the mechanism for determining the framing of the question, determining the timing of the question is not written into the legislation.
One of the gravest concerns I have is the lack of provision in the bill for a double majority. I want to touch on that in some detail because we all know that referenda raise fears. Referenda can be very divisive.
We have had a couple of national referenda, or we might call them plebiscites, in this country in the past. They have been referred to. Mr. Speaker, the time has come for Canada to take the initiative and ratify the Law of the Sea Convention. I believe that by signing Canada will send a clear signal to the world that international law is the way to protect our common economies and environment.

I hear heckles from the New Democratic Party, and I have never attributed common sense to the New Democratic Party. Do not worry, I am not talking about you. It is important the legislation be as fair, as reasonable and as workable as possible. I believe this bill meets this test.

June 4, 1992
Government Orders
In the interests of fairness, disclosure and openness, the bill provides that all committees intending to spend over $5,000 be registered and the contributors and their contributions in amounts over $250 be made public.
The bill also ensures free broadcasting time will be allocated equally to both sides of the referendum question. I pity the broadcasting referee in the Chief Electoral Office who is going to have to make those allocations because it is going to be very difficult. But this is a relatively simple thing compared to what would be required should anybody be insane enough to agree to umbrella committees.
There is nothing in the bill to in any way limit access of all sides to the purchase of broadcast time. As a result, I believe all sides of any question will be able to be put their views fairly to the Canadian public if a referendum was ever held.
I would like to draw attention to the other issue which was discussed in committee. Opposition members expressed concern about the issue of consultation with respect to any referendum question. Opposition parties wanted to ensure there was appropriate advance knowledge about the question. The government agreed with this request and accordingly the bill was amended to ensure leaders of the two recognized opposition parties in the House are provided with the proposed wording of the question and consulted on this wording at least three days before notice of the motion in the House is given. This will ensure a minimum of four days notice before debate begins.
I want to advise the House as well the government agreed to an amendment limiting contributions to referendum committees to sources of financing within the country. This change will alleviate the concern about contributions from non-Canadians including foreign governments, companies which do not conduct business in Canada, and trade unions which have no bargaining rights in Canada.
In another area the government agreed to an amendment which clarifies what is a referendum expense. The change will ensure the normal conduct and responsibilities of members of the Senate and the House of Commons will be specifically excluded from the definition of referendum expenses.
This recognizes the role of the MP must continue during any referendum.
The bill was also amended to respond to a suggestion that provision be made for the text of the question to be made available in aboriginal languages in appropriate locations at the discretion of the Chief Electoral Officer.
The bill as amended in committee addresses the issue for which it is designed. It enables the government to deal with any eventuality, but it should be repeated that no decision to hold a referendum has been made yet. Canada must have every appropriate means at its disposal to defend itself and promote unity.
This is a straightforward matter of prudent management.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to make a very long statement. Nevertheless, I want to express my opinion on third reading of this bill, which is meant to give us a very useful tool in Canadian society, a way to consult the people on something as important as the Constitution.
Mr. Speaker, you should know that in April 1991, our party was the only one that had studied the problem thoroughly and had the courage to submit a comprehen-
Government Orders
sive plan to Canadians to resolve the constitutional crisis which today needs to be resolved as soon as possible because the public is sick and tired of talking about the Constitution.

We decided as a party in April of last year to make a nine-point proposal. When the minister got up in the House yesterday, I was happy to realize that the nine-point proposition that had been submitted by our party, plus the process, has been accepted by the government. In fact we are on the last item of the process, which is the referendum.
Why did we suggest the referendum? It is because the Constitution of the land belongs to the people. That is a very simple proposition. For years we have debated this problem and we see it again at this moment. People are using this occasion to try to bargain something for themselves. When you really talk to the people of the country, they ask why.
This country should have a Constitution. It is very important but it cannot be the only problem we face from now on. It is very convenient for this national government and provincial governments to talk about the Constitution but when you go to the people, they do not want to hear about the Constitution. As a politician, when you make a speech on the economy, the press is there talking about the Constitution.
We are all fed up with that. We know that when the Constitution is in the hands of the people, it will be very difficult for any level of government to use the Constitution as a scapegoat instead of talking about the real problems of the nation.

I listened with care to the interventions that preceded this, and in particular to that of the hon. Leader of the Opposition who said a couple of things I wish to comment on. He said, first of all, a referendum is not proposed as a deadlock-breaking mechanism. I am sure he was not contemplating the government would use it as such.
I think all parties whose members have subscribed to this idea and to this legislation are holding to the recommendations of Beaudoin-Edwards and Beaudoin-Dobbie, which have identical wordings. "We recommend that a federal law be enacted to enable the federal government at its discretion to hold a consultative referendum on a constitutional proposal either to confirm the existence of the national consensus, or to facilitate the adoption of the required amending resolutions." That is not a deadlock-breaking mechanism. It is a facilitative mechanism.
The hon. Leader of the Opposition went on to say, and I believe this is a direct quote: "Whatever happens, there will be a referendum". That is not the intention of the government. The government would much rather this process be seen to a successful conclusion without the holding of a referendum.

June 4, 1992

The whole purpose of having this bill proclaimed into law, as I hope it will be soon, is to be able to use the device of a referendum if absolutely necessary. Mackenzie King was quoted just a moment or so ago, and I would say a referendum if necessary, but not necessarily a referendum, to paraphrase that Canadian statesman.
As colleagues have said, there was very detailed discussion in committee. The bill does not say a referendum must be held or how it should be interpreted. There were 29 amendments proposed in committee. Thirteen of those were accepted in committee or at report stage, and as my hon. friend from Papineau-Saint-Michel has said, seven out of the twelve were Liberal amendments.
It is correct, as the hon. House leader was saying, that there are rather strict limitations on what can be done in the context of 1992 as opposed, for example, to 1980 in the sense we are operating within the atmosphere of a charter today. The freedom of association issue as well as the freedom of speech issue have to be dealt with.
If there are to be umbrella committees that happen voluntarily then that is fine. They presumably would work if they were made to work, but it is our belief to mandate them would be unconstitutional and in some ways perhaps absurd.
With reference to the consultation on the question, I would like to point out not only did we provide a public undertaking to consult the leaders of the recognized parties in the House as opposition parties had requested, but we went a step further. We made that commitment in the bill itself, so it is required now by law as well as by moral commitment, or will be when the bill is proclaimed.
On the issues of financing and the definition of expenses, we have taken the concerns of Canadians into account and have gone a step toward the aboriginal peoples of Canada to make sure the text of the question will be available where appropriate in aboriginal languages.
I would like for a moment to deal with the proposed amendment which was defeated last night and which had
been offered by my hon. friend, the member for Etobicoke- Lakeshore. It is an issue that has puzzled a number of people. What is the appropriate word to describe what we have before us? Is it a plebiscite or a referendum?
Some study on the issue indicates that the word "referendum" and its French equivalent referendum are much more widely understood and accepted, at least in Canada, than the words "plebiscite" and plebiscite. That is particularly the case in the French language. The French word plebiscite is usually given a different meaning. The Quebec legislation which is la Loi sur la consultation populaire uses the term referendum. Using another term in the federal legislation might lead to confusion. To avoid this confusion we might have to use the word referendum in French even if we agreed to the change proposed by my friend, the member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore, in the English version of the bill. While that may be technically correct in French, it might lead to a different type of confusion which we would all like to avoid.
I had the opportunity to meet an international expert on referendums, Professor Francis Delperee of the University of Louvain in Belgium. He has put together one of the most definitive works on the subject. It is titled simply Referendum and has several articles from many countries that have had referendum experience.
I will quote from the Canada section of that work. The article was written by our distinguished colleague from the other place, the hon. Senator Gerald Beaudoin:

There are several types of consultative or deliberative referendums. In the first, the people are consulted; in the second, the people participate in the legislative process. Furthermore, the referendum can be optional or required. In Canada, because the Constitution is silent on this point, referendums are optional.

In other words, the word "referendum" is used in the article by Senator Beaudoin exclusively. He, I submit, is one of the resident authorities.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to review a question I asked during the Question Period of April 20 of this year.
It had to do with the whole economic climate of metropolitan Toronto, a city that used to be an important piston in the economic engine of our country. It would seem to me, as a member of Parliament for York West as part of metropolitan Toronto, the government has either completely ignored the economic fabric of the city or it assumes that somehow metropolitan Toronto is the perceptional fat cat city of Confederation. I am not saying metro Toronto is completely down and out because it is not. At the same time, the government needs to recognize there is also a chronic under-belly to metropolitan Toronto on an economic basis that is in need of some kind of stimulus in order to get that piston operating again, so the engine can function in a much better capacity and put Canadians and their families back to work.
That is essentially the question I asked. The week before I asked that question, the metropolitan Toronto government put out a report suggesting last year alone almost 9,000 Toronto firms either moved out of the city or went bankrupt. As a result of the loss of 9,000 firms in Toronto alone, there was a direct net loss of 65,000 jobs. On top of that another 30,000 jobs were lost as a result of Toronto companies trying to survive by downsizing.
In my own vicinity, the government recently announced it was going to close the Downsview Military
Depot and transfer it to Montreal. An independent study concluded that on an economic basis Montreal was the worst location and the best was Kingston. That meant an automatic loss of 330 direct jobs and also a loss of $106 million in annual contracts that went largely to the metropolitan Toronto area. The number of indirect jobs are probably incalculable but very significant.
When you put the entire package together, it is not one that encourages confidence in the marketplace. It is not one that puts a vibrant Toronto city back to work, but allows it to fester. Confidence is not there and therefore consumer spending is not there.
My question on April 20 is the same one I have this evening. What measures does the government intend to implement immediately so metro Toronto, as an important facet of the economic situation in this country, can return to some degree of normalcy, and the spin-offs we have in metro Toronto as a direct benefit to citizens in Toronto can also be felt in other sectors across the country, and try to begin to put a recovery package in place? It needs some government stimulus or initiatives, rather than a laissez faire attitude, which means the recession will drag on much longer than need be.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to participate in third reading debate of Bill C-74.
At the outset let me say that when my children were very young-and I suspect this is the same for pretty well every other parent on this continent-and they came in with a scratch or a scrape that was not bleeding but was sort of roughed up, they demanded a bandage. The parents complied and gave them a little bandage to put over the cut even though the parents knew it was not needed. However, for psychological purposes the child needed to feel secure and needed to feel that there was some kind of treatment happening.
That is what this bill does. It really is a very tiny band-aid to try to give the impression the government is taking some action to stem or stop cross-border shopping. The reality is there is so much else that can be done to reduce people's need or desire to travel across the border to buy consumer goods. They do it personally as people in my community do. They travel to Duluth, Minnesota; Superior, Wisconsin; and Grand Marais, Minnesota. People in other communities also go across the border to get goods at a price less than they can buy them in their home community.
This bill deals with the symptoms, not with the problem. I regret that the government has chosen not to act seriously about the real problem.

I used as an example two-by-fours produced in Thunder Bay from Canadian trees that were available at a price in Duluth, Minnesota, which was much less than the price at Beaver Lumber that was about one-half mile away from the sawmill. I asked the minister to take a look at those input costs to see what the impact of transportation was, to see what kind of mark-up there was, to see what impact hydro costs had in terms of the over-all costs of doing business in northwestern Ontario, and to take a look at all of the inputs to see if there were any areas where we could do better, where we could be more competitive.
I premised my remarks on the basis that I did not believe anyone in the system was ripping people off, that they were all legitimate costs. The minister never replied.

In the United States there is much more factory to retail outlet direct. In Canada it goes through two or three middle people whether it is domestically produced or whether it is imported. Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to begin debate at third reading of Bill C-75, which has passed committee stage without amendment.
First, I would like to express my gratitude to the members for their co-operation in facilitating the passage of this bill. I am confident that there is general agreement on the nature of the bill, and on the importance of a healthy and vibrant transportation sector in Canada.
This bill amends the Excise Thx Act and Income Thx Act to implement two key measures announced on December 6, 1991 to boost the transportation sector.
The measures included in this bill are a temporary loss offset program with a partial rebate of the federal excise tax on diesel and aviation fuel, and an exemption from
non-resident withholding tax for payments in respect of cross-border aircraft leases. The temporary loss offset program will provide a benefit of $120 million in each of the next two years to transportation firms experiencing temporary cash flow difficulties.
The withholding tax exemption will provide an on-going benefit to Canada's airlines at a cost to the treasury of about $15 million per year.
In December the government also announced changes to the capital cost allowance structure and funding for an institute for research on trucking issues and an owner-operator's trucking co-operative.
These measures, along with the measures included in this bill, respond in a meaningful way to issues raised by the transportation sector. As well, the measures announced in the budget to bolster the economic recovery and build confidence will reinforce the transportation sector as more Canadian goods are shipped to markets at home and abroad.
Response from this sector to these measures has been positive. Of course, this bill does not include everything the sector requested. However, it does provide considerable benefit to transportation in a fiscally responsible way. For example, the temporary loss offset program will yield significant benefits to the transportation sector.
This program provides transportation firms with a 3 cent per litre rebate in exchange for reductions in income tax loss carry forwards. For each dollar rebate received businesses will have to reduce their loss carry forward by $10, reducing future tax deductions.
This 10 to 1 ratio was chosen in order to target the cash flow benefits to those firms that need them most. This targeting will allow the program to deliver significant cash flow benefits while still being fiscally responsible.
I would like to remind the hon. members that maintaining our fiscal strategy is the way to achieve long-term prosperity for the Canadian economy, and therefore for the Canadian transportation sector.
There is an administratively simpler option available for truckers. This option provides a rebate of 1.5 cents per litre of the 4 cent per litre federal excise tax on diesel fuel, up to a maximum of $500 per taxpayer per year. Individual truckers have responded to this program very positively.
June 11, 1992

Although some members of the opposition may differ with the government on certain aspects of these measures it is encouraging that partisan differences have been set aside to ensure the speedy passage of this worth while bill.
It is clear that all parties in this House are in agreement on the importance of transportation to the Canadian economy.
For the information of members, application for the rebate can be made at customs and excise offices across Canada. Application forms will be made available as soon as the bill has received Royal Assent. The sooner this bill is passed the sooner rebates will be received by the transportation sector.
In closing, this bill will provide a timely and substantial boost to the transportation sector while maintaining the government's commitment to sound fiscal management. This is a responsible package of measures that deserves the support of this House.
I urge members to pass this bill without delay.

The driving force behind the Bill C-49 amendments was the need to restore protection for victims of sexual assault in the wake of the Seaboyer decision which struck down former section 276 of the Criminal Code, commonly referred to as the rape shield provision.
Bill C-49 received second reading on April 8,1992 and was referred to a legislative committee for detailed review.

I was struck by the favourable reception given by members to Bill C-49. The same attitude and co-operation were evident during discussions before the legislative committee.
I have said many times, in response to questions about the wording of certain provisions of this bill, that the legislative committee was the appropriate venue for fine tuning the text to reflect accurately the general principles and substance of the bill. I am very grateful to the committee for the attention and care it gave to analysing the text of the bill, and I am also veiy grateful to the many witnesses who came to offer their comments and advice and tell us about their concerns.

Madam Speaker, I am delighted to stand today in support of Bill C-49, on the admissibility of evidence of sexual conduct.
On August 22, 1991 the Supreme Court of Canada struck down section 276 of the Criminal Code, which was commonly known as the rape shield provision, in the case of Seaboyer and Gayme.
Section 276 prohibited the reception of evidence in sexual assault cases of a victim's previous sexual history except in three narrow circumstances. The Supreme Court of Canada held that section 276 overshot the mark in protecting complainants. It held that section 276 had the potential to exclude evidence relevant to the defence and was therefore a violation of sections 7 and 11(d) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. The Supreme Court of Canada suggested guidelines to govern the receipt of evidence of past sexual activity in the absence of legislation.
The decision of the Supreme Court of Canada was swiftly criticized by equality rights-seeking women's groups. It cannot be denied that although sexual assault can be committed against a man the overwhelming majority of victims are women and children. Women feel very vulnerable without the protections formerly provided by the law. While the Supreme Court suggested guidelines for the admission and use in evidence of a sexual assault victim's sexual activity the judgment was silent on a number of issues of great significance to victims of sexual assault.

The proposed amendments in Bill C-49 will clarify the law and the procedure regarding the admissibility of evidence of the victim's sexual activity and will restore essential protection for the victims.
Victim's rights advocates have long maintained that victims of crime are the forgotten persons in the criminal justice system. The amendments proposed in Bill C-49 are an excellent example of how law can effectively respond to victims of crime without jeopardizing in any way the fundamental rights of accused persons. The Bill C-49 amendments are also an excellent example of how the law must conform to current social realities.
The offence of rape was abolished in 1983 and replaced with three levels of sexual assault offences. The trauma suffered by rape victims cannot be so easily abolished nor can the image of the rape victim being once again victimized, this time by the court process.
The Supreme Court of Canada has clearly stated that striking down the so-called rape shield provision does not revive the old common law rules of evidence that permitted evidence of sexual conduct and condoned invalid inferences from it. The rules must be adapted to conform to current reality. The myths that the rape shield provisions sought to eradicate have no place in a rational and just system of law.
The Criminal Code amendments proposed in Bill C-49 will ensure that a rational and just system of law prevails. With respect to the admissibility of evidence of a sexual assault victim's sexual activity with any person, including the accused person, the proposed amendments include a general statement about the purposes for which such evidence may not be used, a new test for admissibility of such evidence, and detailed procedural provisions to govern determinations of admissibility.
The Supreme Court of Canada has unequivocally stated that the fact that the complainant has engaged in other sexual activity with any person, including the accused, should not lead to the inference that the complainant is more likely to have consented to the sexual activity in question nor should it lead to the inference that the complainant is less worthy of belief.
Subsection 276(1) will put this principle into the Criminal Code to ensure that evidence that the complainant has engaged in sexual activity is not admissible
Government Orders
to support an inference that the complainant is more likely to consent or is less worthy of belief.
Bill C-49's single most important feature is the test for admissibility of evidence of a complainant's sexual activity. I would prefer not to use the term "new rape shield provision" but this may be unavoidable.
Proposed subsection 276(2) sets out the test for admissibility of evidence of a complainant's sexual activity with any person, including the accused. The amendment avoids the pitfalls of the former section 276 that was struck down. It does not set out a blanket exclusion with narrow exceptions that the evidence an accused seeks to introduce must fit into. The new test for admissibility places the responsibility of determining whether the evidence is admissible on the trial judge. The trial judge has the task of assessing whether the evidence meets the requirements of section 276.
The questions the judge must ask are: Is it evidence of specific instances of sexual activity? Is it relevant to an issue at trial? Does the evidence have significant probative value that is not substantially outweighed by the danger of prejudice to the proper administration of justice? If the answer is yes to all three questions then the evidence will be admissible.
The task of determining admissibility will not be a simple one. Trial judges will be required to give serious consideration to this issue.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to join with my colleagues from the committee and the Minister of Justice in this debate today on the third reading of Bill C-49.
First I want to say that I was pleased to be a member of the legislative committee. The committee worked very well and co-operatively in hearing the witnesses and extracting from them substantive arguments and some technical amendments. We put them forward and the committee process was one of consensus and co-operation. I am pleased that it was so. I am also pleased that we were able to agree on the amendments and bring them forward.
I am very proud to be part of a government that has made security of women in our society a priority. Our government recognizes that security of the person and the ability to live without fear are essential to women's achievement of equality. We have taken action to ensure that these fundamental rights for women are protected in Canada.
Bill C-49 is evidence of our government's and society's efforts to ensure the security of women who are victims of sexual assault.
Last August the Supreme Court of Canada struck down section 276 of the Criminal Code in the Seaboyer decision which governed the reception of evidence of a victim's sexual history during the course of a sexual assault trial. The Supreme Court of Canada held that section 276 overshot or overstepped the mark in protecting complainants. That decision evoked expressions of concern from many women and women's groups. If assailants could use the provisions of the charter of rights to strike down protections such as the rape shield provision, it would seem that the justice system was offering greater protection to the assailant than to the victim.
The government moved quickly to respond to these concerns. It was a narrow decision by the Supreme Court, but the perception was that women did not have very much protection and, in some cases, they did not. Therefore, we had to move very quickly.
The Minister of Justice undertook an immediate consultative process with women's groups, the bar, provincial and territorial governments and other legal experts to canvass as many views as possible on the direction that the new law should take.

Mr. Speaker, it might reasonably be inferred from the fact that the NDP caucus went along with the unanimous consent to run this bill through the House in its entirety today, correctly in this instance, that it is the intention of the NDP caucus to support the bill at all stages.
That is so principally because, unlike much of the legislation that the government introduces in this House, this bill will do no great harm and may indeed accomplish some small good. The two areas in which we are most interested are clauses 48 and 18.
Clause 48 will essentially prevent land flipping of social housing projects of the sort that we saw for example in Cloverdale in Montreal. A private developer got a bagful of government money on the promise of providing social housing, built a project and then sold it off to people who rammed it into the private sector. The social housing component was gone, the guy kept the bag of money and the new owners are presumably making a great deal more. CMHC was left holding the empty bag. With luck this bill will prevent that sort of thing in the future. To that degree it is commendable.
Clause 18 allows for direct financing of social housing projects by CMHC. It is assumed that this will give CMHC far greater flexibility in its operations and therefore could conceivably allow savings of up to some $150 million over the next five years. This is a best case scenario but we all wish the corporation well and hope that this comes to pass.
This would be a much more significant number and a much more significant hope if the government had shown any intention of financing any more social housing. As we know from the budget presented in this House this year the government's intention is in fact the reverse. It is scrambling as quickly as it can to extricate
itself from virtually all prior social housing commitments.
It merely remains to note that new social housing projects will be cut from their current levels by about 51 per cent over the next two years as a consequence of this year's budget, for example. The co-op housing program is gone completely, and I will return to that in just a moment.
Of course the government is, to be charitable, stalling on additional financing required by those housing co-ops built under the ILM, the indexed link mortgage program, introduced in the mid-1980s. As a result of that program and consequent housing charges imposed by CMHC in an effort to not offend local private landlords, boosting housing charges in the co-ops to a level which the residents cannot afford to pay, there are tremendous shortfalls going on in ILM housing co-ops across the country.
These shortfalls amount in total to a requirement of possibly some $20 million. This too is money that is not forthcoming at this time, which is why some of the more recently constructed co-ops are in serious trouble.
I would like to draw one quick lesson from this, if I may. I do not intend to use up a great deal of House time on this but it seems to me to be instructive that in this bill the government basically is cleaning up the system whereby it can continue to give bags of money to private developers who promise to build housing with some social element in it. This is at the same time the government has axed completely the paltry $6.5 million annual expenditure on the federal co-op housing program and has radically cut back on its commitment to non-profit housing programs.
What this tells me is that the government, in fact, suffers an ideological bias in this regard. It is simply put this way. The government feels better about turning money over to private sector developers to create housing in which tenants will live always under the control of that private sector developer. It feels much better about doing that than it does about funding programs which would otherwise allow tenants to control their own housing.
June 15, 1992

Government Orders
This government lacks faith in the Canadian people. It assumes that lack of money is a clear indication of lack of responsibility and lack of ability. Therefore, because people without money cannot be trusted to devise and maintain and administer their own housing, we must have people of merit evidenced by the fact that somehow or other they already have money to do that for them.
This is the fundamental bias of the government that is expressed in many of its programs and policies across the vast host of issues but is clearly set out in its approach to social housing.
The real tragedy of this is that they could not be more wrong. Anyone dispassionately examining the record of co-op and non-profit housing in this country versus the record of housing provided with government assistance through the private sector, especially tenant housing, cannot conceivably come away from such a dispassionate examination concluding other than that if you put the responsibility for their own housing in the people's own hands you will have a more responsible, better administered, longer life and better maintained housing than you will if you place them in a standard tenant relationship to some private sector landlord.

Government Orders

The member from Ontario, let us say. What Jean Barteski was saying was that the switch to retail outlets is helping destroy rural Canada. Let us put a stop to post office closures.
Finally, I have a letter from Mr. Glen Smith of Saltcoats. He says in his letter: "Quite a number have been closed in our riding and one supposes the rest are at risk in Saskatchewan. Rural Canada needs these jobs and this federal presence".
Once again, here is a gentleman talking about the federal presence disappearing because of the closure of the post office. The flag is gone, the federal presence is gone, the community gathering point is gone, the service is deteriorating, the consistency of the hours is not necessarily there. The fact that we will lose jobs is also a key point.
All of these rural post offices have a postmaster or a postmistress. They all need a back-up person, part-time help, and it is a real asset to a small village, town or hamlet to have a few extra part-time jobs in terms of the economics of the community.
Often it is one family with children who go to school. It provides extra economic input into a small community. With the closure of the post offices it is gone.
Finally I want to say that if one looks at the statistics we find that in this country since 1984 there have been 1,239 post offices closed. One hundred and seventy-four of those have been in the province of Saskatchewan, roughly 15 per cent for a province that has around 4 per cent of the population of Canada.
If we add the number of post offices closed and those under review, there are now 1,595 closed or under review across this country. Two hundred and thirty-one of those are in my province of Saskatchewan, again a much greater share than we should have in accordance with our proportion of the population in Canada.
I cannot agree to support this bill. It is a bad bill. The post office has failed miserably in providing a decent and reliable service to the people of this country.

June 18, 1992
Government Orders
The whole objective of the post office is to run at a profit. It is the wrong priority, the wrong objective. First and foremost the post office should be a service to all people in this country, regardless of whether we come from a large city, a small town, a farm or a fishing village in Newfoundland, it must be a service to the people of this country, provided at the same cost for every citizen of Canada. That is the whole philosophy behind the post office and behind a postal stamp.
With those words I want to encourage the House to hoist and defeat this bill. It is not good for Canada. Hopefully the Conservative Party will join us in making sure this bill is done away with. It is a bad bill for the country.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I rise as the NDP justice critic to speak on this bill, one in a long series of justice bills that we have been debating in this House.
This is a ticketing scheme for minor regulatory offences. Currently, just to explain how the law works, a person wishing to plead guilty to an offence, even one as minor as picking flowers on federal property or speeding in an inlet or lake, must appear in court. Even in that person's absence, if the person does not appear, a trial must be held and witnesses must be heard. It is an expensive and time-consuming process.
We have an alternative method of doing things. We have ticketing offences in the provinces, traffic tickets for example. Bill C-46 proposes a ticketing scheme for minor regulatory offences and was designed primarily for the following reasons.
First of all, it decriminalizes minor offences against federal laws and regulations. As my friend pointed out, not the Criminal Code but other federal laws and regulations. Second, it avoids the need for a court appearance when a ticket is not contested. Third, it encourages improved enforcement. I might add as a Scotsman it is probably going to end up a little cheaper.
Bill C-46 does not create new offences. It only changes procedures that deal with existing minor federal offences. We are told that the government expects there will be over 400,000 tickets issued in the first year this scheme comes into effect. These fines will be paid. They will go into general revenue and so they will not be an additional means of raising funds, say for Agriculture Canada or Environment Canada. Savings will be realized as a result of a decrease in demand placed upon our courts. It seems like a good idea financially.

June 18, 1992
Government Orders
I spoke on the bill in the House at second reading and I will not repeat that speech. It was on Monday, April 6,
1992.	In case members want some bedtime reading tonight, they can get Hansard and have a look at it.
One point I did make in the speech and I will reiterate was that this idea which we all agree now is a good idea and is going to save the government money and streamline the judicial process was first introduced in 1976 by the Law Reform Commission of Canada. That is the same Law Reform Commission the member previously said the government is going to abolish.
It was doing good things. This is another argument to buttress the opposition's point of view that it really was not too intelligent to get rid of the Law Reform Commission of Canada because it advanced some of these ideas that ultimately became law. Here is a perfect example.
I should say also that I was impressed with the way the civil service and the committee brought forward the bill in a straightforward way and said when they did not know the answers that they did not know the answers. That is why I am prepared to agree. I was prepared and did agree to a pilot project in this matter.
Mark Berlin of the justice department notes that all provinces have a similar program in place. It is probably a result of provincial representations that the federal department is taking the initiative.
They did hint at a few things like using credit cards, Visa cards, and various ways to pay fines. I do not know how that is going to work. I told them not to get too fancy. Look at how the provincial traffic schemes work and try to follow that. Do not get too fancy or you will end up like the post office.
I will end with two wishes. As the member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys pointed out, a lot of this law, as many laws, is in the regulations. I hope the regulations will see the light of day. I hope the department will publish them, show them widely, so that we can change them and make them better.
Finally, my last wish is this. I know it is a bit late to do this now but I have a bill in front of the House called the Plain Language Act in which I have asked that the government draft bills in plain language, plain English or plain French. It is too much to expect us to speak in plain language in the House but the government could draft in plain language. The government might want to have a
look at future bills, especially the regulations under this bill, and draft them in plain language so Canadians can understand exactly what is meant by the regulations. This would be a good bill to begin with.
I have talked about plain language, about open and competent regulations and about how important it is that this bill pass because it is overdue. It will make a better process and I hope a cheaper process for Canadians. Having finally got to the end of a long series of justice bills, I am pleased to sit down and to shut up. In plain English I say I am finished speaking and I hope this bill will pass.

-all introductory and related speeches, be printed as an appendix to
House of Commons Debates of that day and form part of the records

I note that on all previous occasions beginning in 1941 when heads of state or governments have addressed this House the speeches have been printed in Hansard. For example, the speech by Mr. Herzog, President of the State of Israel, to both Houses of Parliament on June 27, 1989 was printed as an Appendix in the Commons Debates of that day.

The Canada clause is not ringing poetry, but it is a way to try to put on paper what it is that we think Canada stands for. I think that is a particularly important start for a sense of nationhood for us in the future.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to rise in this debate to support the referendum question and the Charlottetown accord of August 28. I do so with enthusiasm and commitment.
It is true, as many other members have said, that this accord is not perfect, but neither was the the British North American Act of 1867. It went to the Supreme Court and the Privy Council thousands of times. I am not overestimating that, thousands of times. That Constitution and the society it founded, the country it founded, lasted for 125 years.
If the people in 1867 had nit-picked at that Constitution like many of our people nit-picked at the Meech accord and at this accord, we would never have had a country. They had the political will to form a country and to adopt a Constitution despite its imperfections.
I say to this House that despite some imperfection in this accord, it represents many substantial gains for many communities in this country. What are they? To begin with, for the first time constitutionally we have recognized the inherent right of the aboriginal peoples to govern themselves. Those are landmark, world precedent, provisions. We should be proud of them.
If it were only for those provisions alone in the accord I would go to the wall in support of that accord because those are so important all by themselves.
For the first time constitutionally we have recognized the minority language communities in our Constitution with a commitment to their vitality and development. I say for the first time we have recognized the official language communities because in the Constitution of 1867 and in the Constitution of 1982 we recognized the right of individuals to go to court in English and French, to have schools in English and French, but we do not refer to the communities, to the collective rights.
This is the first time that we have said we recognize the collective rights of the communities, the francophone communities outside of Quebec, and the anglophone community in Quebec.
I must remind the House that there are now over one million francophones living outside of Quebec in this country. There are more francophones outside Quebec than there were in Quebec in 1867. There are 800,000 or more anglophones living in Quebec, which is more people than many of the provinces.
Again, these provisions represent a substantial gain for those communities.
Third, the Charlottetown accord contains several provisions that recognize the distinct society of Quebec and assure not only its continued existence but its epanouisse-ment and development.
This accord, without doubt, contains much more than the Meech accord to protect the unique position of Quebec. I cannot understand why those who supported the Meech accord, like the hon. member for Lac-Saint-Jean and the other members of the Bloc Quebecois who at that time were in the Conservative Party, would now attack this accord when it contains much more than Meech.
If we put the Meech accord side by side with this you would see that eveiything that was in Meech is here, plus the guarantee for Quebec to keep 25 per cent of the seats in the House of Commons-which it historically has always had more or less so this is not something new, but it is now written in the Constitution-plus a guarantee that they will have one-third of the judges in the Supreme Court of Canada, plus a veto with other provinces on changes to national institutions, plus a double majority in the Senate to protect language and culture at the federal level, plus greater clarification and consolidation of provincial powers.
Again there are definite gains, not all that people in Quebec would like but substantial gains to protect the language and culture and the future of Quebec within Confederation.
Fourth, this accord gives more clout to the west and to the Atlantic provinces through a reformed Senate. It is true that it is not a Triple-E Senate, much to the disappointment of many people in the west. I would have supported a Triple-E Senate. However, it is a two and a half E Senate. It is an elected Senate. It is an equal

Senate and it is almost an effective Senate. That remains to be seen.
It is true that the Senate will only have a total veto on matters relating to resources and on matters relating to the French language and culture, but its power to force joint sessions with the House of Commons on other matters will have more significance than many people expect.

He was born in Ottawa in 1903 but at five years of age his parents moved to the Pembroke area where his father worked for years in a local sawmill. As a result, Paul came from very humble beginnings up the Ottawa Valley. He came from a family with a strong faith and a strong caring attitude.
His father was a great source of encouragement to him and his mother was always there to give him some veiy wise advice. He always told me she played a tremendous role in moulding his life.

The Liberal Party met to choose a candidate for the provincial election of that year and it ended up with no candidate. At the end of the meeting one of the good old-timers got up and nominated someone he considered to be a very bright young man from Pembroke by the name of Paul Martin who was at that moment a student at law school. Everybody agreed Paul should be their candidate.
The next morning they phoned him at university and told him he was the candidate for the provincial election. His father also learned the next morning that his son Paul had been nominated to run against none other than his own employer and that created a little bit of difficulty for a while. The Martin family in its entirety was very proud of and loyal to Paul Martin.
Tributes

Our hearts go out to them today because they were always there, they were very proud of their brother Paul. They worked hard, particularly Lucille, to give Paul some help in his education.

Mr. Speaker, I really wish it were that easy.
I am going to refer to my notes because I have a number of points I want to make, particularly with regard to the question of rail grade separations and its logical extension to rail safety.
As of January 1989 with the proclamation of the Railway Safety Act, the railways of this country have had their primary responsibility for safe rail practices clearly established and brought up to date. The federal Department of Transport monitors railway operations and it is empowered to take action to correct any threat to safety of the public or railway personnel.
Our two major railways, CN and CP Rail, had the best and the third-best safety records respectively, of all major North American railway companies in 1990.
However, this does not mean to say that there will be any reduction in the monitoring of their operations. The department has every intention of completely fulfilling its obligation to ensure that safe procedures are followed.
Despite the commendable goal put forth by the hon. member opposite, I feel that we can make the taxpayers' money go a lot further with a well thought out and balanced program of grade crossing improvements and public education than we can by assigning huge amounts of money to a comparatively few grade separation projects.
The reality is that Transport Canada's grade crossing improvement program provides an immediate safety dividend at a relatively low cost at many locations across Canada. For example, it takes approximately $80,000 to install an automated light and bell warning system at a level crossing. Installation costs for flashing lights, gates and bells are about $150,000. The total cost to eliminate grade crossings by contrast is positively immense.
To use an illustration, CN Rail's 534 kilometre, high density main line between Montreal and Toronto has 135 grade crossings with active warning systems as well as a large number of crossings with passive systems including public, private or farm grade crossings. The total cost of building grade separations on this line alone at an average cost of $8 million each would be in the order of
$1 billion. This figure does not include pedestrian crossings.
There are more than 24,000 public grade crossings in Canada, 8,000 of which are equipped with automatic protection devices such as flashing light signals, bells or gates. The balance is protected by standard cross-buck grade crossing warning signals. In addition, there are some 33,000 private or farm crossings which are for the most part unprotected.
Prevention of accidents at grade crossings requires action by motorists, railways, road authorities and the federal government. Therefore, an example of where responsibilities must be accepted is the establishment and maintenance of clear sight lines to enable drivers to see approaching trains. Although this measure is cost effective, it is sometimes difficult to get the responsible party to carry out line-of-sight clearance. While the railway responds relatively quickly to orders to clear brush along the rights of way, municipalities may resist a similar request to clear railway lines in their jurisdiction.
Under the Railway Safety Act, the Minister of Transport has extensive powers to improve grade crossing safety to help prevent accidents and to initiate remedial measures after an accident. Railway safety inspectors also have considerable discretionary powers to act in the interests of safety. It has used these powers to impose speed restrictions on both the railway and the road authority where it feels it is necessary to limit risk.
It has also required road and/or railway traffic to stop before proceeding through a crossing and, where a severe threat to safety exists, it has actually closed crossings. An exceedingly important component for safety at railway crossings rests with education.
Transport Canada contributes $150,000 a year to the Railway Association of Canada's Operation Lifesaver, a public education program that promotes safety at railway crossings. A recent survey done for Transport Canada has shown that the public is generally unaware of the inherent dangers at railway crossings. Much of Operation Lifesaver's public education campaign, therefore, will be directed at the areas targeted by the survey in coming years.
Transport Canada does not just talk about safety, it spends a fair amount of money. There is an $8.5 million program in place to improve grade crossing warning systems. The department pays up to 80 per cent of the total cost of railway crossing improvements and the

balance is provided by the railways, municipalities or provinces.
These improvements include the installation of automatic warning devices such as flashing lights and bells, the interconnection of devices to highway traffic signals, lighting, improvements to the road approaches, to track layout, clearing of line-of-sight and construction of a road or rail detour. There have to be choices made every year as to which projects proceed and which must wait.
The criteria used to assess these projects try to address this frankly tough process as fairly as possible. Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I will try to be as brief as possible because I truly believe that this debate belongs
in the House management committee rather than on the floor of the House, but it is here and we must deal with it here.
On April 29, 1992 the House of Commons concurred in the 28th report of the House management committee and this report dealt with standing order changes regarding legislative committees.
On May 7, 1992 the House management committee passed a report which stated: "That further to the motion adopted by the committee on June 18, 1991, the subcommittee composed of the three Whips be delegated all authority to act as striking committee pursuant to Standing Order 113, and provided that the report recommendations are unanimous it present them directly to the chairman of the committee for presentation to the House on behalf of the committee".
This allowed the striking committee to bypass the House management committee in order to table reports on the membership of legislative committees. The clerks of the House management committee needed to put in place a process whereby they could get consent on membership from the Whips and get the reports into the House.
Up until this point the Whips were able to do the same thing by submitting the names of the members from their own caucus to the clerks who would put together a list. The list would then be circulated among the Whips for their signature and then returned to the clerks. The clerks then put together a report for the chair to table.
This was thought to be a rather cumbersome process and so after the above motion was passed the clerks consulted with the Whips and decided on a new process. Again, briefly, it goes like this. The Whips submit the name of the member to sit on the committee along with the Whips' initials. The clerks can immediately put together a report for the chair of the House management committee to table.
Problems arose with this as well. The office of the New Democratic Party Whip regularly sent over names of members without the initials of the hon. New Democratic Party Whip. The clerks would send the notice back and ask for the initials. Sometimes this would take a few days. The clerks began to submit reports without the New Democratic Party Whip's initials.
November 19, 1992

At least three cases are on file with the clerks' office in which the hon. New Democratic Party Whip did not initial his submission. The reports were tabled and deemed adopted without incident. Those reports were: the 40th report, Bill C-73; the 46th report, Bill C-79; and another report which number I do not have but it was with reference to Bill C-78.
Thble clerks have told us and it is my judgment that if the committee chair feels that the committee report is in order and he or someone on his behalf tables the report it then is in order.
If the opposition raises a point of order on the matter I believe the Chair should not entertain arguments because as far as I am concerned the committee report is before the House. If the Whips are unhappy with that, I submit is a committee problem and must be dealt with within the committee.
I did have an opportunity to consult with the chair of the House management committee yesterday evening and he confirms the facts as I have outlined them. I regret that he is out of the city today and not able to be in the House, but I can assure the House that the view as I have outlined it was confirmed by him in a conversation I had with him yesterday evening.
