That, in the opinion of this House, the government is incapable of providing leadership and direction in the economic and social affairs of the nation and has lost the confidence of this House and of the Canadian people and that, therefore, an election should be called forthwith, in accordance with the Canadian custom, practice and tradition of holding a general election at least every four years.

November 20, 1992
Supply
This motion was put forward by my esteemed colleague for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell. It is most important and very serious.
In 1983 the current Prime Minister stood in this House and declared: "The government should honour the fundamental British tradition in this country which calls for an election, not in five years, but within four years, so that people can judge the action of the government".
I whole-heartedly agree with the Prime Minister in his comments. I also must congratulate him for sticking to his principles the first four years of his mandate as Prime Minister of this country. He launched the 1988 election by declaring: "It has been a Canadian tradition to call an election after a government has completed four years of a mandate".
One would expect any principled individual to do the same thing four years later, but unfortunately this same Prime Minister has decided that there are things greater than principle. Even more unfortunately we have seen this Prime Minister and his Conservative colleagues cast aside principle on too many occasions over the past eight years.
The latest polls show the popularity of this government at only 22 per cent. I would like to take the time today to outline some of the things which have caused Canadians to lose confidence in this government.
First and foremost is the economy. It has been totally mismanaged by this Conservative government. The inaugural issue of Canadian Business Economics reports that tax increases since 1984 have been historically unprecedented in magnitude. The increase in the tax burden in Canada was by far the largest among the G-7 countries of the world.
Thxes on the household sector in this country saw an increase of 6.7 per cent of gross domestic product between 1984 and 1991. Comparatively in the United States, the increase was only 1.3 per cent. Furthermore the additional tax burden borne by the average Canadian family will be an increase of $1,894 in 1992.
It is well recognized that the major challenge facing Canada today is that we must become more competitive in today's interdependent and highly competitive global economy. However, some serious disturbing signs of
Canadian competitiveness and our weaknesses have emerged over the last 10 years. Specifically, in relation to our major international competitors, growth in our manufacturing productivity and technology performance-two key indicators of competitiveness-has been quite poor. Our ability to compete in today's changing world economy is being eroded, not the least by the amount of the national debt that Canadians are financing.
Canada's merchandise trade surplus has fallen from $19.8 billion in 1984 to $11 billion in 1991. Canada's current account balance has gone from a $2 billion surplus in 1984 to a deficit of $27 billion in 1991.
Canada's share of world trade slipped from 5 per cent in 1979 to 4 per cent in 1989. Canada only has 2.6 per cent of the world share of trade in high technology products, compared with 3.5 per cent in 1971. Canada's labour productivity has grown only 1.8 per cent between 1979 and 1989, compared with 5.5 per cent in Japan and 3.2 per cent in the United States. Canada has lost over
200,000	manufacturing jobs over the past 30 months, and most of those jobs were here in the province of Ontario.
In order to meet the demands of globalization, some important restructuring in industrial economies is necessary. Unfortunately the government has not taken any steps to meet these demands.
Canada needs a policy which both acknowledges economic change and which helps Canadians adapt to these changes. Recognizing the link between free markets and government is one step toward accomplishing this goal.
Liberals advocate a global trade policy driven by Canada's strategic trade priorities which reduces our dependence on the United States and which would endeavour to make Canada the first global outward oriented economy on the continent.
Liberals recognize that trade policy must be closely associated with domestic policy. Monetary fiscal investment, training, education and research policies must be linked together with our trade policy. The Conservative government has failed to recognize this need. It has also failed to recognize the need to rethink attitudes toward issues such as education and training, research and
November 20, 1992

development, interprovincial trade barriers and labour management relations.
The Conservative government has failed to realize that education, research and environmental policies are the building blocks of economic growth. These failures have caused serious problems for Canadians from coast to coast.
The current Prime Minister of Canada told this House in 1983: "It does happen that a government sits too long. It does become exhausted and it does become bankrupt of ideas''.
I think Canadians everywhere recognize the truth of those words. This Conservative government has lost the confidence of the Canadian people. An election should be called. Canadians have suffered enough.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I do not totally disagree with the suggestion of putting massive amounts of money into infrastructure. I do not think anyone, even on this side of the House, would totally disagree with it. The difficulty obviously is how much is enough, and where do you find the money? That is the problem that I guess we as a government face. It is a tough one.
We use the old term ourselves, even though sometimes we hate to hear it, kick-start the economy. Going back to what I had previously mentioned, that would be fine if our debt load were not as high as it presently is. There is no problem with that. The problem is when you step through all the engines of the economy, if you wish, the private sector-that is the engine-the corporate sector, and you might say the individual sector, all of those things have to be working to make the economy work.
You know there is a very, very high debt level, and that is the problem. How much do you use? In a sense, when you say how much do you use, you are asking how much do you borrow to make it happen.
Here is an interesting statistic. We talk about the time that we took office and what we have for an accumulated debt today. Let us forget about whose fault it is. We will continually blame each other, no matter how long this House sits. Anyway, we all agree that today it is somewhere in the vicinity of $400 billion, give or take a few billion. But let us say it is $400 billion, which it is. Today it consumes about 31 per cent of all revenue, just paying interest on that debt load of $400 billion.
If we had followed on the old course with the spending habits of the previous government, and with due respect not too many of us in this House were in that old government, none of us on this side at least, statistically we would have a debt load now of $900 billion, close to
one trillion. There are so many zeros on the end of that one you need a half-ton truck to carry them around with you. We would have a debt load of about $900 billion. This is the important part to remember because it would not be consuming 31 per cent of revenues to service the interest on the debt, it would be taking over 60 per cent of those revenues. Then you have lost control. The International Monetary Fund moves in and governs Canada, if you wish. That is the difficulty.
That goes back to the premise of the member's question. How much do we borrow to throw into the economy to kick-start it? The honest to goodness truth is that I am not sure we can afford to borrow any more. I think we have got to find the money somehow. Personally, I see the solution to the problem as simply this: The international world and the corporate sector do have a fairly high degree of confidence in Canada. The difficulty now is that we do not have confidence in ourselves at the consumer level.
What I see happening in Canada today, and you can blame it on a number of things including, if you wish, our tax structure, is that consumers in Canada are not spending and retail tax revenues are going to be down. My guess is, based on what I see happening, they are going to be down by about 13 per cent. Therefore, the best thing that could happen in Canada would be if consumers started spending. It would generate enough revenue that the government then would have enough movement to do something without borrowing more money.
I think part of the solution to the problem rests with ourselves. When that confidence reaches a certain point and Canadians start spending, I think we will be on the road to recovery because the other fundamentals are there. That is happening south of the border, it is starting to happen here and we hope that it continues to proceed along that way.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take the opportunity to respond on this group of amendments. Like my friends across the way, I will tend to do it by referring to Motions Nos. 10, 12 and 13 together, 11 and 22 on their own.
On Motions Nos. 10, 12 and 13, I want to say, and I know that many people in this House recognize it, that the principle of reasonable grounds in criminal activities are well established in this country, not only for the Criminal Code, the tax act and the competition legislation but it is something that requires a well established objective basis.
In the past, the courts quite clearly have made decisions along this line. To suggest that it is simply government responding to rumours would not stand up in any court and would not be reasonable in any government administrative process under Bill C-86 or any other legislation.
In terms of proposal No. 11, it suggests that we would only be able to keep people out that are members of prescribed organizations. In discussing this at length in the legislative committee, one of the expressions I used then which I think is appropriate at this time is that while it is impossible always to know the nature of an immigrant or of a refugee that you might want to bring in in the future, it is equally impossible to be able to know and therefore define all of those people that you are going to want to exclude in the future.
I understand when my colleagues often talk about clauses in legislation which sometimes are too wide open and perhaps cast too broad a net. But I also have come to understand the real problem that we have when we quite clearly start trying to go too far to define. In our attempt

November 23, 1992
Government Orders
to be prudent and fair, we find ourselves in a position where we work against not only the interest of the country but against those who choose to come to the country.
On Motion No. 22, which involves the discussion that my colleague had about the question of the interest of Canada, I want to make two comments if I may. First of all, this particular clause, clause 28 of this bill which will be section 38.1 of the new law when it is in place, is a purpose clause. It provides, as my hon. friend from Notre-Dame-de-Grace has said, for the setting up of sections 39 and 40, which provide for the certification process in recognition that you do not want to have too much power without the proper checks and balances.
This legislation provides for a certification process under the provisions where there is a threat to the country. Both the minister of immigration and the Solicitor General must sign a certificate and that is what this process allows for. Certainly there is protection provided in section 6 of the charter that relates to the same thing.
The second point is that the interests of Canada are not always clearly defined but sometimes they are readily evident. Unfortunately we have seen in this country from time to time those who have come here and co-ordinated or undertaken activities that have nothing to do with things in Canada but with other countries.
For instance, if there was an effort to carry on a plan of terrorism or subversion in another country from Canada it is certainly not a threat to the security of Canada but it is a threat to the interests of Canada.
One thing this particular section of amendments addresses, which is sometimes very difficult for some of us to come to grips with, and I find myself in this bind often, is the question of balance. We constantly must balance the interests of Canada and Canadians with our responsibility to not only provide the opportunity for those who want to come to Canada and contribute to this country but also to provide safe haven and refuge. Certainly in my view that is the greater responsibility that we have.
The balance comes in ensuring that we have a system that is fair, accessible and open and continues to allow Canada to live up to its tradition of being a protector without parallel around the world, while at the same time ensuring the security of Canadians and the immigration refugee determination system by knowing who we have in the process and by being able to deal in those very rare situations with those who should not be in this country. Until now in some cases the minister and the department have not had the ability to remove people from this country when I think any reasonable person would say they should be gone. That is what some of these provisions provide for.
I suppose we could sit and imagine situations where there would be a negative effect, where provisions could, if we examined them in isolation, be used against those who choose to come to Canada. That has not been the tradition in this country. That is not the way the Immigration Act has been used, either the 1976 act or the 1988 act. I do not believe there are many who believe that is about to change.

minister's office and often we could get that decision reversed. This bill works against the ability of members of Parliament, especially those in urban areas, to do their job properly and effectively.

The Minister or the Deputy Minister, as the case may be, may authorize such persons employed in the public service of Canada as the Minister or Deputy Minister deems proper to exercise any of the powers and perform any of the duties and functions that maybe or are required to be exercised or performed by the Minister or Deputy Minister, as the case may be, under this Act or the regulations, other than the powers, duties and functions referred to-

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have this opportunity to debate a topic of such importance to the future of our immigration program.
The objectives of Bill C-86, the reunification of families, the protection of refugees and the promotion of economic growth were in fact in danger of being seriously compromised by the system's increasing inability to handle the convergence of pressures and by the related erosion of confidence Canadians were expressing toward our immigration programs and objectives.
In this climate, the government understood from the outset the urgent need for a constructive and open examination of the methods, processes and criteria we use to select and bring people to Canada. We understood as well that this examination had to involve as many Canadians as possible. That is why the government
Government Orders
undertook the most broadly-based and yet focused consultative and educational immigration strategy in Canadian history.
These open-ended consultations dealt with such critical issues as the number of immigrants we would accept over a five-year period to meet our domestic needs and international goals; the speed with which we should bring immigrants to Canada in the context of our ability as a nation to handle the increase and the best way to integrate newcomers into our society.
As well, the past eight years have seen other significant developments, including a gradual and controlled increase in over-all immigration levels, a parallel expansion of the services essential to integrating new Canadians into our way of life and a long-overdue overhaul of our refugee determination system in response to historically unprecedented pressures on the program.
These amendments clearly provide Canada with the tools to manage change in the 1990s. A common thread running through all the consultations, deliberations and debate on Bill C-86 has been an acknowledgement of the need to manage our immigration program more effectively, with greater fairness and with greater relevance to the needs of Canada as a whole. This is what Bill C-86, as now proposed, sets out to accomplish. Specifically, the proposed amendments offer a rational, workable formula to manage change in three distinct but interrelated areas of immigration policy.
First, Bill C-86 provides the means to further streamline our refugee determination system to ensure that fair decisions are rendered and rendered quickly.
Second, Bill C-86 would better protect Canadian society by tightening enforcement and control measures to defend the integrity of the system and protect the public from those who would abuse our programs or break our laws.
Third, under these amendments we could select effectively those who come to Canada through improved management of the categories and numbers of immigrants, thus ensuring that immigration continues to contribute to our social development and economic prosperity.
If I may, I would like to touch very briefly on each of these three crucial areas.

November 24, 1992
Government Orders
I believe everyone here today and most Canadians understand the need to streamline our refugee determination system. Quite simply, the time required to process claims and make decisions is still too long and that is not fair to legitimate claimants.
The speed with which we can remove rejected claimants remains slow and that erodes the effectiveness of the system. The consequence of all the delay is further pressure on costly support programs and that certainly is not fair to taxpayers.
The co-ordinated changes proposed in this bill will serve to create a more workable, clear-cut and streamlined refugee determination system. These changes include, among others, the elimination of the first level or credible basis hearing which was proving ineffective, improvements at the immigration and refugee board level to accelerate processing, cuts to administrative costs to allow genuine refugees to more quickly become part of the community, new procedures to expedite the landing of convention refugees with cuts of up to six months in the waiting time for landed status, and more timely, effective and fair removal procedures in cases where claims have been rejected.
The impact of these changes, including faster family reunification and a more efficient decision-making process will only enhance the special position Canada has in the world for its work on behalf of refugees. Complementing these changes, Bill C-86 proposes measures to better protect our immigration system from abuse.
At our borders we will give immigration staff the power to search individuals and to seize documents and vehicles used in smuggling operations. We will expand the authority of our immigration officers to fingerprint and photograph refugee claimants and increase the penalties for people caught smuggling. The net result of these efforts will be to more clearly distinguish between those who should benefit from Canada's generosity and those who should not.
Clearly, in a decade that promises continuing international volatility, large-scale movements of people and economic uncertainty, the ability to more effectively manage our immigration system is a priority. The changes Bill C-86 proposes will ensure that our immigration program can deal with change while fulfilling its time-honoured role as a contributor to national growth and prosperity.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin by making a few comments about why we need immigration to Canada.
I am sure all of my colleagues on both sides of the House as well as Canadians in general will agree that if we are not to allow immigration to Canada, by the year 2011 we will start to see a decline in terms of our present population.
To that extent that will pose a tremendous challenge to both the government as well as to the people of Canada in terms of the shrinking tax base in Canada. Simply put, by the year 2010 we will have almost double the amount of people on the retirement role in terms of people who are receiving pensions. We will have a shrinking in terms of the work force and, as such, we will have less taxes being paid to the government coffers.
That by itself is a good reason why we have to look for means and ways in order to do two things: first, continue to provide the quality of services to the people that they are accustomed to. At the same time, that will be good reason for us to say that without immigration, we will not be able to survive as a nation for very long.
The hon. member mentioned the fact that the vast majority of immigrants to Canada come from Third World countries. That is true and I want to tell him why. Simply put, it is because historically immigration to Canada has always been from countries where they have depressive regimes, a lack of economic opportunities, civil wars and so on.
All these people who have come to this country since the very early days up until now have come from countries where opportunities were not available. Certainly another factor why we are not getting immigrants from Europe is because Europe is faced with the very same situation we are faced with. That is a decline in terms of the population in Europe. The birth rate in Europe is in the same category as that in Canada. They do not have enough production in terms of population in order to sustain the population growth.
That is why we do not see many people coming from Europe to Canada. The other reason is that they have good opportunities in Europe and there is no reason for them to emigrate.
Government Orders

Private Members' Business

The Royal Canadian Legion has made it very clear, very plain. Last April Comrade Fred Williams wrote to the Prime Minister and stated that the Royal Canadian Legion most strongly requested that any new bravery award system included provision for the permanent retention of the Victoria Cross as Canada's highest military award for valour.
We can do no less. I urge my colleagues from all parties to put this legislation through without any wrangling about it, and I do not think there will be. This is one area where all parties are unanimous in support of this bill. Mr. Speaker, just a short recap on what these motions are about.
In the February 1992 budget, it was decided to wind up the International Centre for Ocean Development. ICOD was doing some of the same functions being done by CIDA, the Canadian International Development Agency. The role of ICOD does not require that it be a separate organization. This is why the government decided to wind up ICOD and transfer its resources to CIDA.
The resulting savings in overhead, some $3.3 million, will be redirected within the official development assistance envelope for programming. CIDA will take the appropriate measures to ensure that assistance in relation to ocean resources continues to be provided to developing countries.
The work of ICOD has been accomplished with a staff of 74 and an annual budget of $13.3 million. At the government's request, ICOD and CIDA have prepared a wind-up plan for approval. The plan which was approved by Treasury Board outlines a fair and humane severance package for ICOD employees and the transfer of necessary working files to CIDA and the arrangements for ICOD's existing contractual agreements. For example, ICOD has contracted its programming activities to the Consulting and Audit Group of Canada pending parliamentary approval of dissolution. After dissolution, CIDA will assume this contract.
In conclusion, the government's decision to wind up ICOD will mean more aid for international programming for developing countries. It will mean less overhead and a rationalization of the government's department and agency portfolio.

There has been a great deal of discussion both here and outside of this Chamber, regarding the role of judges in our legal system. They have very little or no opportunity in their current incarnation to have input into public policy in the research and development way. They have the ability to write decisions on those questions put to them in the courts and in the normal way if they happen to be appellate court judges. Obviously there is a limiting factor there.
Other levels of the judiciary, particularly those at the most active level in dealing with the public, which are known in my province as provincial magistrates, have no opportunity of the kind my hon. colleague mentioned.
I have risen many times in this House and discussed the need for mandatory training of judges, for example, in gender sensitization. I would hazard a guess that if the Law Reform Commission were still in existence, a number of judges would see the problems with gender sensitization, not just within their own brethren and sisterhood, but across the board in our society because of the cases they face. Indeed, they have now lost the opportunity to input this kind of data into a body such as the Law Reform Commission.
There is another area of great concern to Canadian women that would have been an area the Law Reform Commission would have studied. That is the whole area of sexual harassment. There is not a woman in this country, Madam Speaker, and I know you agree with me on this, who has not had to deal with this pernicious development at some time in her existence.
This week I have twice raised a situation in this House relating to two of my constituents, members of the Public Service of Canada, who have lodged a complaint founded on sexual harassment. I also raised this point last week.

Mr. Speaker, the area of occupational health and safety is the responsibility of the provincial government and is not the jurisdiction of the federal government.
Notwithstanding this fact, the Government of Canada, consistent with its role as a financial guarantor, took several measures to ensure the Westray project was technically viable. It is the responsibility of operators and regulators to apply that knowledge base in developing control strategies. We put the steps in place consistent with our role as financial guarantor to ensure the company was in full compliance with the provincial regulatory standards on health and safety.
This was monitored on a monthly basis by an independent mining consultant.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the hon. member when he talked about us silencing our critics.
I would like to remind him, for example, that the Economic Council of Canada predicted that the free trade agreement would bring, if I remember the figure correctly, either 200,000 or 300,000 jobs over the course of many years. That figure was used by the government, by business and so on, in support of arguments for the free trade agreement.
The Economic Council of Canada-and certainly it may have criticized the government in some areas-was supportive of the government in many other areas. This is not an issue of silencing critics. This is more an issue of Canada being a mature nation with mature universities today, many of which are over 100 years old. The university from which I graduated, the University of Alberta, celebrated its 75th anniversary a few years ago. It is probably celebrating its 80th anniversary now. There is a source of research for us and we have other institutions.
My question for the hon. member has to do with the role of Parliament. For years and years Parliament and the governments of the day have created these external agencies asking them for advice, but it seems to me that Parliament itself should be a policy-making body or policy should emanate from Parliament. We do not have enough committees studying the role or producing policy recommendations.
We have reformed Parliament. The McGrath commission in 1986 reformed Parliament. It would seem to me appropriate that maybe we should now consider beefing up the research bureaus of our committees, unleashing the potential of members of Parliament and restoring some of the esteem the public should have in Parliament, rather than always devaluing Parliament by spinning off policy-making agencies and think-tanks and
Government Orders
people looking to those groups as agents for social change and other things rather than to Parliament. I think Parliament should regain its role as a policy recommending body and committees should try to increase their stature in that manner, and many have done that.
Does the hon. member think that Parliament's role has been devalued by having this plethora of different agencies? Might we now re-assert ourselves as parliamentarians, give our committees extra power and produce policy recommendations in that way?
My next question concerns the economic argument here. These agencies cost a lot of money; $5 million is a lot of people paying taxes. We have to borrow that money. Then each year we have to pay interest on that borrowed money and we have to borrow money for interest. There is a never-ending, vicious cycle of compound interest, debt and so on. Certainly we could pay heed to some of the recommendations of the Auditor General, but that would not solve the problem of our massive debt and continuing deficit.
The Liberal Party and the NDP have called for increased spending every day. I sit in the House of Commons and every day I hear calls for massive programs, economic stimulus and so on. All that does is create inflation in the long run and devalue our currency and productivity.
We have to think seriously about the economic course of the nation, about the public purse and about keeping things on an even keel so that people have productive jobs.
We certainly have eliminated these agencies, but how do we get the deficit in check? What suggestions does he have on the big ticket items? His party seems to be saying: "Spend more, spend more, spend more". I will leave it at that and ask him to respond.

Anyone who has been following the real world over the last two decades recognizes that this has become a major factor in all parts of the world, not just in Canada but in the United States, Britain and throughout Europe.
The bill we are looking at today, Bill C-26, represents the first significant change to the Public Service employment legislation in more than 25 years and as such it is long overdue.
I would like to talk today about one of the key features of Bill C-26 that was raised by the previous speaker, that is deployment. Before doing so I would like to spend a few minutes to set the scene to provide the context in which we developed the proposals we are debating today.

The Public Service experienced tremendous growth, exponential growth, as new employees were added, but times have changed.
We are no longer able to add these new programs and hire hundreds of new employees to service them. We have had to and we still have to learn to maximize our resources, to get the most value from our dollar, to be more efficient and indeed more productive. To use the oft-repeated phrase, we have do to more with less.
That is the reality that not only our Public Service managers face today, but also all of the employees within the Public Service. We have to give them the tools that will allow them the ability to meet that challenge.
Managers in the Public Service will tell you and so will
many of the employees that the staffing system is complex, cumbersome and time consuming. They will tell you there has been far too much emphasis on process, on faithfully following the prescribed steps on filling in the necessary forms. Managers will tell you, as they have told the Auditor General, that the staffing system as it currently operates is a serious impediment to effective management of the Public Service.
There is another very important factor. That is the need and the aspirations of the Public Service employees themselves. Public servants understand full well that the opportunities for advancement are more limited than in former years. However, they want the opportunities to learn new skills, to try out different functions, to meet new colleagues and clients. They want to be stimulated and motivated by new challenges and ideas.
We need to provide them with the flexibility to access these opportunities. This is not only so the employees can fulfil their own aspirations, but also because we recognize that employees who have a wider range of skills and abilities are more adaptable and more able to meet the challenging needs.
Our employees have tremendous potential, potential that in far too many cases has gone untapped. It will benefit all Canadians to unleash that potential.
In Bill C-26 we have tried to provide a reasonable balance between the need for greater efficiency and flexibility in our systems, to respond better to the needs of the public and to the legitimate aspirations and interests of our employee to develop their knowledge and skills so that they can continue to enjoy challenging careers. nery and telephone. Furthermore, the Speaker shall table before the House of Commons the statements of expenses on any of the first 30 days after the statements are deposited by the members with the Board.
The Board of Internal Economy, as created by the Parliament of Canada Act, is responsible for financial and administrative affairs concerning the House of Commons, its premises, services, staff and members.
The board may make bylaws to regulate members' use funds, goods, services and premises made available to members within the context of their parliamentary functions. It may also make bylaws concerning management and accounting of funds made available to members. The Speaker shall table these bylaws in the House of Commons within 30 days after their approval.

The Parliament of Canada Act provides for sessional allowances for members of both Houses of Parliament. It also provides that any member of each House of Parliament shall be allowed certain expenses, such as moving, travel, transportation and telecommunications expenses.

Mr. Speaker, I rise in the House today to explain why I cannot support Bill C-98.
Basically, this is a bill that authorizes the government to borrow, that provides additional borrowing authority for the modest amount of $8.2 billion.
Many of our listeners or viewers may find it hard to understand why the government has to borrow this amount and why it has to keep coming before the House to ask Parliament's permission to borrow. Perhaps it would be easier if I compared today's exercise with someone using a credit card. That someone is the government. Our government has a credit card. In fact, I call Bill C-98 the MasterCard bill.
The government has just realized it overspent. Its MasterCard credit card is already up to the limit: $447 billion. So instead of cutting its spending and getting rid of the card, the government has decided to go out and borrow more money, and to do that it needs the authorization of Parliament. Of course, we in the NDP, and the Liberals probably as well, will vote against the bill, because when a government or an individual is unable to control his spending, we have to cut off their source of income and say: Whoa. You haven't learned your lesson, and until you have, we are not going to give you more money than your initial budget called for. I am sure my colleagues in the consumer movement in Quebec and members of family savings co-operatives would agree with this approach because that is what they have been teaching Quebecers for a long time. It is too bad the government did not take advantage of the advice available from the people in these grass-roots organizations in Quebec because I believe Quebecers are very good at managing their money and staying within their budget. The trouble is, the government is not.

February 2, 1993
Government Orders
I wanted to know what the $8.2 billion the government wants to borrow will be used for. In the economic and fiscal statement presented on December 2, 1992 by the Minister of Finance, the government made three promises, not six, about the way it would spend our money. The first promise was, and I quote: "We will continue to invest in policies that make our economy work better". Quite frankly, is giving $5 billion to Hibernia a policy that will make our economy work better? Is wasting $50 million on Canadian Airlines really a policy that will make our economy work better? I don't think so.
The government's second promise is about the way it will spend the money, and I quote: "We will further strengthen our investment in people". People, my foot. I could talk about the cutbacks in unemployment insurance. Especially in Quebec, people are very upset and that includes the Conservative caucus. The hon. member for Chicoutimi is very upset about this and in fact a number of Conservatives are upset about these cuts in unemployment insurance. We have trouble understanding how they can cut money for the unemployed but give more for various pieces of equipment like helicopters and so on for the Department of Defence.
That is not all. There is also the tough, painful dispute on labour force training between the federal government and Quebec. They say: "We will strengthen our investment in people," but that is not what they are doing.
The third promise is this: "We will make additional investments in public infrastructure". Yes, but where? When? How much? Where are some specific examples of this famous public infrastructure? Personally, I have not seen them.
I come to the fourth promise in the budget: "We will continue to invest in broadening trade opportunities". I am in favour of trade but before talking about free trade with Mexico and all that I would really like more free trade among the provinces. I remember that when I was
on the Beaudoin-Dobbie committee one thing this government promised was to make Canada a country where there was free trade among the provinces. But we do not have that yet and we never had. It is really ironic to see all that in the pamphlet or brochure that the Minister of Finance distributed.
The fifth promise, still telling us how they will spend money: "We will continue to invest in sound monetary and fiscal policies". I do not think that our present monetary and fiscal policies are sound. This government has not kept to its budget since it took power. We have had two finance ministers and so far we are $447 billion in debt. That is certainly not a sound monetary and fiscal policy.
Finally, I quote the sixth promise that they say they want to keep: "We will invest in partnerships with the provincial governments, workers and business". As far as workers are concerned I have already told you about the cuts to unemployment insurance. I can tell you that is a joke which Quebecers do not find funny. There was no partnership.
When Bill C-91 on pharmaceuticals was tabled all the provinces except Quebec were against it because they knew that drugs would cost more as a result. I am not proud that my province, Quebec, was in favour of it because ultimately, this bill is at the expense of the most vulnerable people.
In closing I must tell you that this government is bankrupt, not only financially but also in terms of leadership and vision. That is even more serious because one can always find money somewhere but a government so lacking in leadership and vision deserves a slap from the voters and I hope it will get it soon in a federal election.

No, in 1987. The first one of its kind to be published by any government in the world. Although provincial departments across the country approved these guidelines, they are neither compulsory nor binding. However, it is expected they will help individuals and public agencies to be consistent in their assessments of the need for corrective action. In the longer term, these national guidelines will be used as a basis for developing or modifying the building code, standards for construction materials and furnishings, and ventilation requirements.
The department developed these guidelines in June 1980 when the Ontario Deputy Minister of Health requested a federal-provincial study that would set standards for air quality in new residential housing projects. A proposal to form a task force on indoor air quality was officially tabled at a meeting in October 1980 of the Federal-Provincial Advisory Committee on Environmental and Occupational Health. I mention this so that people who are interested will realize there are a number of committees and that a number of things have been done in recent years. The deputy ministers of health subsequently approved the proposal. The advisory committee created the federal-provincial task force on indoor air quality, whose mandate would be to examine a definition of acceptable air quality, the need to establish acceptable objectives and maximum acceptable concentrations of specific substances, and standards for ventilation or air recirculation. The scope of the mandate was restricted to residential establishments and the task force was to make recommendations designed to protect the public, based on constant exposure, in other words, 24 hours a day.
When it wrote these guidelines, the department wanted to protect the health of the great majority of the general public, including groups at risk like very young children, the elderly and persons with known health problems. These groups are especially concerned with indoor air quality because, as we know, they spend most of their time indoors. The department set itself two major objectives: (1). To develop guidelines on the concentrations of particular air contaminants in homes, taking account of factors like the sensitivity of groups at risk and the sources and modes of action of the contaminants; (2). To develop as much as possible other guidelines or recommendations on measures to protect or improve air quality in domestic establishments.
The federal-provincial task force met for the first time in September 1981 under the aegis of the Department of National Health and Welfare. In the next four years it collected and examined scientific documentation on 18 substances or groups of substances before setting the guidelines and recommendations contained in the document published by the Minister of National Health and Welfare in April 1987.
The government agreed in principle to update the guidelines in 1992-93 so that is now going on. The group will consider other substances to be added to the guidelines. If it seems possible to develop guidelines on these substances the work will again be facilitated by the Federal-Provincial Advisory Committee on Environmental and Occupational Health.
That is why the very existence of these guidelines, combined with the research now under way in various federal government departments, shows that we have implemented a national strategy for reducing the threats posed by exposure to contaminants in indoor air.
Also, our government's tobacco policy is another measure that has particularly improved indoor air quality in public buildings. Nevertheless, it should not be taken for granted that everything is going well. As a member of Parliament when I was Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, I had to deal with the case of a citizen who is fighting a constant struggle throughout the country with the problems of asthma and the possibility that he might have to work or even live in buildings that are insulated in different ways.

I have no confidence that the cod stocks are going to miraculously reappear in two years time. I wish that could be the case. We all wish it. However it is wishing and not doing anything concrete that has us in the difficulty we are in right now.
I can recall when the current minister of fisheries, at that time the minister of trade, said that he would not allow the cod quota to be reduced to 190,000 tonnes because it would be tough on Newfoundlanders and would create unemployment. The experts were saying it should be 190,000 tonnes or perhaps even less than that but the current minister of fisheries insisted that the quota stay at 260,000 tonnes.
That was the beginning of the trouble. I said at the time that it was short-term gain for long-term pain. I was much more prophetic than I realized at the time.
The member for Fraser Valley East spoke about the great progress that is being made and about the co-operation of the European Community. I can recall travelling to Europe with members of the committee in 1989 when representatives of the European Community told us that as long as we were harvesting the stocks the way we were and as long as we were not obeying the recommendations of our experts to cut the quotas seriously they were not going to pay any attention to the quotas either.
Now we are certainly paying attention. We have stopped fishing and that should have been done earlier than it was. We have demonstrated that we are prepared to take this measure in Canada when it is shown that there is no other alternative. We are doing it. We are proving to the world that we are doing it.
NAFO is agreeing. It has always gone along with us. It is the European Community that has not. One member of NAFO, the European Community, has not paid any attention to all the quotas that have been set. It has exceeded them regularly.

Mr. Speaker, I enjoy the opportunity of entering into this debate dealing with Bill C-93 and only regret that it had not gone to committee before Christmas. However, after a couple of days debate it is time now to move ahead and get it to committee so it can be dealt with in detail.
I rise to enlist the support of members of this House to ensure swift passage through second reading of the legislation which is before us. I am particularly interested in part (e) of the bill, the merger of the Procurement Review Board of Canada with the Canadian International Trade Tribunal.
This merger streamlines government administration through the creation of a new entity called the international trade and procurement tribunal, or ITPT, which will combine the strengths of the Cm and the PRB and report to Parliament through the Minister of Finance.
The merger also paves the way for an improved bid challenge mechanism that more suppliers of government procurement need that can be used to appeal contracts they feel have not been awarded fairly. In fact, the legislation positions the ITPT to meet all of the government's current and future bid challenge responsibilities.
For the short time that the free trade agreement has been in place and considering the limited scope imposed upon the PRB under the free trade agreement, the PRB has under the guidance of the former chairman, Gerry Berger, and the present chairman proved to be an inexpensive, speedy and even-handed alternative to the court system.
Indeed, they have set up an impressive set of laws, regulations and policies which ensure that suppliers will be dealt with fairly. Now suppliers seeking recourse when they feel they have been denied a fair opportunity to bid have found the PRB to be an extremely responsive vehicle.

Government Orders
In fact about 5,000 Supply and Service Canada procurements out of almost 300,000-about 2 per cent of our procurements each year-fall within the scope of the FTA. These are all potentially subject to the PRB and the PRB has handled some 95 complaints since its inception in January 1989. The majority of these were raised by Canadian suppliers who felt they had been unfairly treated.
Indeed, as a result of the decisions, if read, you will find that about one-third of those have been sustained to the point that they felt the procurement had not followed the rules laid down by government legislation and regulation. This gives a good opportunity for the suppliers to bring their complaints and indeed for procurement officers in various federal government departments to be more aware of how they should handle their procurements in a level playing field.
Suppliers tell us they are pleased with the transparency of this quasi-judicial review authority. It brings a good bit of honesty to the federal procurement system. They have also appreciated the board's informal and expedient approach. Complainants have felt that the PRB dealt with them fairly and they have appreciated not having to incur the time and expense of court hearings.
The board has given short shrift to frivolous complainants. It has not been used as a delaying or leveraging tactic, nor has it been used to distort the competitive market.
Similar to the Procurement Review Board, the guiding principles of the ITPT will be to promote an open, fair, impartial and transparent procurement process. The new tribunal will function in a timely and effective manner with the powers to receive complaints, conduct inquiries and to make determinations.
Naturally the ITPT would first assume the PRB's former role so that the merger does not disrupt the service to suppliers and Canada will continue to fulfil its obligation under the FTA.
However, many companies in industry associations have suggested that a similar form for redress should be available to suppliers on a broader range of federal procurements, indeed federal procurements which we make just within the government and are open to only
Canadian suppliers. The legislation before us opens the way to such a forum.
If we are truly committed to ensuring the integrity of fairness of government procurement then we must also be committed to ensuring that it is capable of withstanding independent third party scrutiny.
At the federal level we have already taken a number of steps, for example through the open bidding policy to achieve greater access, fairness and openness for all potential suppliers. Open bidding was an important and welcome development for suppliers. Simply put, more businesses can now access the federal market. There was nowhere to go to complain if one of them thought there was something wrong with the way the contract had been awarded.
The only avenues were through the departments, first of all to the procurement officer who perhaps awarded a competitor the contract, then to the deputy minister and then to the minister. With this new system the people will be able to direct it to an arm's length, third party tribunal, which will give them a fair hearing.
As I mentioned earlier, the first obligation under the FTA will be continued and then the broadened bid challenge mechanism would be introduced, which would encompass purchases covered by Supply and Services Canada's open bidding policy.
That is all the contracts which Supply and Services Canada puts out to tender of over $25,000. Generally speaking, that is good and makes sure that the playing field will be level for all suppliers. That amounts now to more than $4 billion annually that we opened up for challenge under this new mechanism.
We will set up this broadened bid challenge mechanism by establishing regulations that will allow appeals of these contract awards to the ITPT.
The introduction of such an appeal mechanism will be a landmark event for Canadian companies that supply goods and services to the federal government. It would challenge the whole federal procurement system to be squeaky clean.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, non-insured health benefits or health services are provided to registered Indians and Inuit in Canada by the medical services branch of the Department of National Health and Welfare.
Some services include the provision of prescription drugs, medical supplies and equipment, transportation for medical reasons, vision care services such as eyeglasses, and dental care. The non-insured health benefits program is designed to help registered Indians and Inuit reach a level of health comparable to that of other Canadians.
February 25, 1993

Adjournment Debate
Non-insured health benefits of various types have been paid for and provided to registered Indians and Inuit by the federal government for many years. In 1979 a variety of policies, practices and guidelines were replaced with a new Indian health policy. This was based on three principles of community development, the traditional relationship of the Indian people to the federal government and the utilization of the existing Canadian health system.
Since 1979 national non-insured health benefit program expenditures have increased from $36 million to over $400 million in 1992-93. Eligible beneficiaries have increased from 325,000 registered Indians and Inuit in 1979 to 560,000 in 1992.
Because of criticisms about the lack of adequate management and control of non-insured health benefits programs, Health and Welfare Canada was asked by Treasury Board and the Auditor General to make concerted efforts to implement administrative improvements.
This has been accomplished by the development of directives and administrative procedures coupled with the development and implementation of a health information and claims processing system under a contract with Ontario Blue Cross.
First Nations were informed of the changes and officials of the Department of National Health and Welfare met on numerous occasions to describe the changes and inform First Nations leaders and communities of the program. Workshops have been held in many regions at regional, tribal and community levels.
The Manitoba First Nation leaders have taken the position that the directives are an attempt by the federal government to define treaty rights unilaterally. Manitoba chiefs have also claimed that implementation of the automated claims processing system by Blue Cross is a move to transfer federal responsibility to the private sector.
The position of the federal government is that the program is derived from the Indian health policy and changes to it in no way prejudice or are intended to prejudice treaty rights. The federal government retains full control of the non-insured health benefits program and Blue Cross is merely providing administrative support for an automated system to process claims and provide information on benefits utilization.
The system is operating and functioning well in Ontario, Saskatchewan and Quebec. Health and Welfare Canada did not have the capacity to operate the automated process and pay the bills. It decided to identify a company with the capacity to develop and operate the system through the normal Supply and Services Canada tendering process. Open tender was called from the companies with experience in the area of health insurance. A significant number of companies indicated interest and attended the bidders conference. Four of those companies or groups submitted tenders from which the successful bidder was picked. Blue Cross was the successful bidder.
Health and Welfare Canada is committed to self-government and has approached First Nations leaders to discuss the development of a framework with which non-insured health benefits can be considered for transfer. One of the prerequisites of central agencies prior to approval being given to the transfer of this program is that the costs should be within control.
The automated system allows the department to demonstrate the real costs of the program. This information allows for accurate forecasting expenditures and the development of a formula or formulae for allocations upon transfer.
As soon as these parameters are developed and agreed upon, transfer authority will be sought.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I rise as a follow-up to a question I raised with the Minister of National Defence on February 16. It concerned peacekeeping.
The tenor of the question was based on the concern and observation that there are a number of red flags being thrown up regarding the manner in which we deploy our troops, the risk that is under way and the strain on personnel resources and operational maintenance resources for the remainder of the Canadian forces. The fact that these operations take place without consideration in Parliament I believe is the overriding concern.
Another reason for the concern and the real reason I am here tonight is that I see the Canadian forces participating in peacekeeping operations because of their excellent record in this regard and because of the understandable desire of any government, including our own, to participate and continue to participate given the condition of the world today.

February 25, 1993
Adjournment Debate
There is a point when I believe discretion has to be used. Peacekeeping in the last four years has more than doubled. In fact more peacekeeping operations have taken place or been generated in the last four years than in the past forty and I do not see that decreasing. I will tell you why. There are 179 countries in the world today speaking 4,000 languages. I think 60 of them have a population of one million or less and 40 of them have a population of less than 200,000. More importantly, less than 10 per cent of these countries have a homogeneous ethnic population and less than 5 per cent have an ethnic group that accounts for more than 75 per cent of the population.
Therefore what you are in fact seeing is an explosion of nation states downward to the point where they are really comprising the smallest ethnic or religious groups.
In fact it is tribalism. These forces of tribalism and nationalism are intractable forces. I think you are going to see more and more of it as time goes by.
If you add to that the low level of tolerance that seems to be dominant in the world today for religious, social and ethnic differences, then I think that is another nail in the coffin for more peacekeeping operations.
I should really call them peace operations because, Mr. Speaker, as you are well aware, the United Nations is now responding to peace operations in many ways, not just peacekeeping in its traditional sense as we know in the Cyprus operation in which we have been involved for many years.
There are things like humanitarian assistance as we have in Somalia, guarding food convoys as we have in Bosnia and indeed such things as election monitoring as we have in Cambodia. None of these operations, despite the heroic efforts of the men and women in the field, appear to be moving with a great deal of success. That is another reason why we have concerns.
I merely want to follow up on the minister's response which touched on the business of some time in the future being discretionary only because we will have run out of resources. I trust that my remarks will have some influence on the minister and indeed on the government
as they make future decisions on committing our forces to peacekeeping operations.

Mr. Speaker, it is a real pleasure to speak to one of my part-time constituents, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. He has a residence in Kaleden which is in my area. I hope he will be able to vote for me in the upcoming election. I know he realizes that I have been telling the truth about this government and that I have done a good job in this area. He even hears that from members of his own party in Penticton which I am always heartened by.
Let me just point out to the minister as well as to the people in my riding and the rest of Canada that what the minister has not told us is that since this government came into power Canadians are paying approximately $1,858 more every year in federal taxes than they were in 1984.
Look in the estimates to see what this government has done with respect to seniors. It has chopped the Seniors Independence Program and cut the New Horizons Program by 40 per cent, a program that has been well used by seniors in Okanagan-Similkameen-Merritt as well as the rest of Canada.
He talks of inflation control. Just last Friday in my riding office I was speaking to a senior woman who brought in her old age pension cheque. She explained to me that she had received an increase in that particular cheque of $2.17 over the previous period. I tried to do what the government would do. I explained to her that the inflation rate had dropped and that the Old Age Security was tied to the inflation rate.
She mentioned to me something I already knew and which I would like to pass on to the minister and the government. That rate is based on the food basket and other things. In her area the cost of her housing has gone
Government Orders
up something like 15 or 16 per cent over the last year, yet she received an increase of 1.2 per cent. Her heating and utility bills have gone up substantially. The cost of food and related things has gone up. Therefore, her cost of living has gone up 12 to 15 per cent over the past year. However, she was receiving based on the cost of living index across Canada an increase of something like 1.3 per cent on her Old Age Security cheque.
That is the reality of what is happening to the seniors community in my riding and I would suggest the seniors community across Canada.
I dealt with the tax rebates and I know exactly what happens. If the minister were to look at the statistics he would see that often the tax rebates in some cases and in some income levels, yes, are up and above what would normally be paid out in taxes. I do not deny that. My point is that as predicted what is happening is that as these quarterly payments come in people are so up against the wall they are using them to purchase necessities of life.
Recently because one woman had to call in a plumber she did not have sufficient money by the end of the month to buy food for her three children. The GST rebate is being used for things such as that.
The minister mentioned that passing on the taxation was a mortgage for our grandchildren. Let me point out to Canadians and to this minister that under this government our national debt has more than doubled. We are now $460 billion behind the eight ball. Look at the budgets over the last two years. We see predictions of a year and a half ago that our deficit this year would be $22 billion. In October last year, a scant eight months after the last budget, we saw that the prediction was $34 billion.
Now we are hearing sounds from the Minister of Finance that our yearly deficit will be over $34 billion because of this government's monetary and fiscal policies even though the interest rates have dropped, saving this government a couple of billion dollars in interest. This government can still not face up to the fact that it has made a mess of its tenure in office. It has made a mess of the finances of this country. This government is leaving a negative legacy for our grandchildren.

March 12, 1993
Government Orders
I have this to say to the government: Shame on you, good-bye after the next election.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of State for Finance and Privatization, or the minister of "it's quite a state we find ourselves in today", is either totally ignorant of the problems facing Canadian steel makers or he is being conveniently evasive. On top of that, this government should not have rushed headlong into negotiating a North American free trade agreement when there was unfinished business. In particular the Canada-U.S. free trade deal resulted in Canadian steel makers being charged with dumping in the U.S. The verdict of guilty being handed to us by the U.S. against our steel industry shows how the FTA has failed this country.
My question is simple. Does the minister truly believe that the Canadian steel industry, with the problems I have just outlined, would be any better off today under NAFTA than it was yesterday under FTA? Or is the minister going to rely, as this government so often does, on the market forces to prevail and on the market to look after itself? We can see that the big brother government south of us is definitely going to have an upper hand on our steel industry.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words on the report stage of Bill C-113.
I want to congratulate my colleague, the member for Timmins-Chapleau for the excellent amendments he has introduced. I want to particularly address my remarks to Motions Nos. 16, 17 and 18.
The first thing that strikes me, and it has struck a lot of people who are familiar with the way unemployment insurance works, is that a person who applies for UI has a two-week waiting period. Often it takes longer than the two-week waiting period for the agents at UI to collect all the relevant information so the decision can be made on the application. Often it will run to three or four weeks. The client does not get cards and certainly does not get any cheque from UI. The client may get a response from UI eventually as to the disposition of his or her application.
My colleague has introduced a very logical amendment to ensure that time limits are adhered to so the decision is rendered to the claimant within the two-week waiting period.
By law the employer must provide the claimant with the separation certificate. If the employer does not, it has to be reported to the commission. This can cause a considerable amount of delay because the claim cannot be set up until the separation certificate is received.
The way it works now, the client informs the commission that he or she has been unable to get the separation certificate and the commission then goes after the employer. If the employer does not provide the separation certificate, the employee is asked to bring in the pay stubs and a claim is set up based on those pay stubs. That all takes time.
Government Orders
With the advent of new technologies in the processing of applications and the computerization which has taken place, surely it is possible to adhere to a two-week waiting period as my colleague has suggested. If the employer does not come up with a separation certificate in two weeks, then a claim would be set up for the client based on the stubs if the claimant has them, or some verification by the client of what his or her pay was. The claim is set in motion for the claimant, and the employer is dealt with according to the law if he has not provided the separation certificate or other information that is required. I think this is a very appropriate amendment and I do not think it will create any problems on the part of the UI agents or those who process the claims. I think it is quite possible to have a two-week period within which a decision is made and rendered and the claim is processed.
It seems to me that my colleague's Motion No. 17 requires the commission to maintain statistical data. I understand that when the committee held hearings my colleague asked witnesses for statistical information about those who were disentitled without good reason. He asked what those reasons were.
He discovered that 190,000 clients were disentitled without good reason in 1991. When he asked for the statistical information with respect to the reasons Mr. Gordon McFee, who is the director of policy and legislation development, Department of Employment and Immigration, told my colleague that the precise reason for the disentitlement of these 190,000 is not coded but the fact that the claim was adjudicated negatively is. The way one comes up with the 190,000 figure might have been a simulation.
Decisions are being made on amending the Unemployment Insurance Act in Bill C-113 which are not based on information. The government is not able to determine whether the information on which it has based its proposed amendments is really appropriate because it does not have the statistical information. My colleague asked if one could assume theoretically that some of the reasons given for leaving employment may have been valid even though a negative decision was reached. He was told that was possible and there may have been negative decisions given for reasons that were totally appropriate. They may have been just, but we do not know that because we do not have the statistical information.

Government Orders
I want to address a couple of things specifically, however. The first is on trade. There is no doubt that the cornerstone of any trade policy has to be the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade. In terms of the North American free trade agreement our position is that this agreement should only proceed once Canada is satisfied that through parallel accords we have corrected the shortcomings of the original deal. Our trade critic has expressed this many, many times in the House. He asks very responsible questions every day in expressing what we need.
What do we need specifically? First of all we need to improve the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement in reference to the subsidy code. We need also to recover some of our losses in the energy area. We all know that. We have spoken on those extensively in the past. There is insufficient protection for the environment in the North American free trade agreement as it is. The Americans have recognized that and the new administration wants a parallel accord. The problem is that the government across the way says it does not need anything and the accord is fine as it is. We do not agree.
The member asked about the goods and services tax. Here is the position we have taken. We know as a government-which we hope to be very soon-we are going to need the funding necessary to function and to continue to provide for the social programs that we as a party invented a number of years ago. We know we will need the money from some place. It is not just swell to say we will abolish the GST and not replace it with anything. That is not very responsible or cute. Of course we do have to replace it with something.
The Leader of the Opposition has stated that he will appoint a committee of this House to travel right across the country to develop a program within 12 months after the government is sworn into office so we can replace this tax. Yes, there will be another tax but it will be one that works and does not take an army of accountants to figure out and does not provide the burden that this present taxation regime does on small and medium sized businesses in my riding and elsewhere in Canada.

Canada Post had two important governmental decisions to make since it was created. When Andre Ouellet was the minister responsible for Canada Post, he made the first decision to privatize the postal system. It was a good decision.
Why did the government want to privatize the postal system then? It was to take from the House of Commons all sorts of decisions that were to be made about postal services and rates and other matters.
The other good decision about Canada Post was made after 1984-85, when the minister, Harvie Andre, told them: "Too bad, but starting now, you will have to cover your costs and come up with a corporate plan so that Canada Post will not depend on the government every year for the $200, $400 or $500 million you need to balance your budget".
One thing is clear, Madam Speaker. Why do we have postal services? To take a product and send it somewhere else at the lowest possible cost. Before, we would send the product somewhere else, but sometimes that was expensive and this was discussed in the House of Commons. Taxpayers watching us said there was no way they would pay 45 cents, so we told them we would charge 20 cents for sending the item and the government
would subsidize the remaining 25 cents. It still came out of the taxpayers pocket, but that didn't matter.
Basically providing postal services means taking a product and sending it somewhere else as quickly as possible and at the lowest possible cost. In 1985 the government told the Canada Post Corporation that the lowest possible cost of sending a product to Vancouver, for instance, was the real shipping cost. In other words, do not count on the government to subsidize potential deficits.
Of course there was a risk because Canada Post was practically in a monopoly position and people were afraid it would become a monopoly and would make decisions without regard for the interests of the general public. However that was not the case. It did not become a monopoly, on the contrary. Personally I think that soon we will have fewer and fewer post offices, unfortunately perhaps in terms of the federal presence. Why? Because it is not a monopoly. Look around Ottawa or Montreal or other major Canadian cities and see the services of priority post as well as those of other companies being used every day. I am thinking of Federal Express, Purolator and United Parcel Service, and they even have aeroplanes with their own logo to carry the mail. There is no longer a monopoly as there was before.
Second, we now have fax machines. Some post offices could close altogether and use fax machines to send the same letters, provided the addressee has a machine as well. We no longer have a government monopoly, but a Crown corporation competing with other companies with different prices and costs.
We are still sympathetic to consultation, but consultation is not necessarily what people will do because the decisions made concerning Canada Post always lead to emotional situations. Just look at what is happening right near Riviere-du-Loup, where the people are rising up against Canada Post because it wants to close the post office. Any platform is good. If there were an advisory board to review this decision, I am not sure the debate would be more elevated or more dignified because it would be in the House of Commons.

The current act is so full of loopholes that it enables a trust to continue to roll over and over. Just by simply changing the trustees under the existing statute the 21-year period is revived. The government has settled that issue with people who have existing trusts by cutting

back on the deferral period to the deferral allowed for the first generation removed from the settlor and the tax applies on the death of the first generation.
Currently, because of the ability to roll it over and over with each succeeding change in trustees, the 21-year rule that is supposed to be a terrible rule that will prevent the government from collecting all sorts of money is a massive loophole for the wealthiest families, as my friend from Kamloops said. We have closed that massive loophole. I am at least pleased that the member for Sudbury has recognized the government's positive action in that regard.
We have made arrangements for these trusts to terminate when the youngest or the last person or whoever is immediately the beneficiary related to the first generation from the settlor dies.
There are two kinds of trusts. There are trusts set up in wills and most of the trusts that are dealt within this statute really are trusts set up by people who die. When they die the capital gains is paid on their assets and then their assets are put in trust for the beneficiaries. The trust can run until the death of the beneficiary if the beneficiary is one beneficiary removed from the testator and that is the end of it.
It does not require winding up a trust in a 21-year period but it allows the trust to run its normal course. That seems to me to be very fair. As I said, most of these things are put together by people in their wills. They are testamentary trusts.
Some trusts, however, are set up by people who want to do major inter vivos settlements. When a person does an inter vivos settlement he or she has to pay capital gains tax on all assets that have been put in trust. To the government that is a bonus because it gets its capital gains tax in advance when the settlor sets up the trust. The government does not have to wait until the settlor dies.
Some people suggest this is a great advantage to the settlor. I suppose an advantage is an advantage if it is perceived to be an advantage. It may not be an advantage at all because the settlor is paying tax to the government sooner than he or she would normally have to pay it. To the government that is an advantage. To the government the sooner a person pays tax the better, as pointed out by my friend from Kamloops. This might be perceived by some to be a great tax loophole but frankly on balance it

is no loophole at all. It is just the payment of tax perhaps earlier than the government might normally expect it.
I recommend this statute be left as is. We did not hear in committee, despite the evidence of Mr. Goldstein and Professor Neil Brooks, any real justification for changing it. The member for Sudbury who has made the amendment we are speaking to now recognizes the advantage of the changes proposed. I suggest we carry on recommending the advantages of all the changes rather than just being selective. I think the statute should pass as is and the amendment should be defeated.
